1818473,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.5.1.1.2,1955-07-20,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,ATOMIC ENERGY,URANIUM ORE,INQUIRY AS TO PURCHASES BY GOVERNMENT,Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with particular reference to a statement made in this house on July 15 as recorded on page 6214 of Hansard in response to a question by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). On that occasion the Minister of Trade and Commerce in response to a question about the production of uranium ore replied in these words:

It seems to me there is plenty of uranium ore being produced: at least, we have undertaken to purchase all the finished product that is produced in Canada up to the present time. At the rate new discoveries are being made, how long we can continue in that position I cannot say.

My question relates directly to a report in the Globe and Mail of this morning under the heading ""Ottawa will purchase all uranium produced between now and 1962"". That is based upon a report from some unnamed

official stating that the government will purchase all uranium concentrates produced in Canada until 1962. The statement is not attributed to the minister. As the report indicates, considerable uncertainty is created because the impression was left by the statement of the minister that it might not continue until that date, whereas this statement declares that purchases will continue until 1962. As I said, this statement is by an unnamed official and it may not be accurate, but I believe that the importance of the exploration and production work associated with uranium, and its extent, makes it highly desirable that the minister should clarify the situation, and I ask him if he would do so now.
Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade

and Commerce): There is no foundation for the statement that the government will purchase all uranium produced until 1962. Each project is treated separately. There is consultation between the atomic energy commission of the United States and the officials in Canada. If the project commends itself as being one that can be underwritten by both countries-I may say that every contract made is underwritten by both countries -the project may be underwritten. But there is no present guarantee that all purchases will be underwritten by the government.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Alexander Drew,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce&Language=E&Section=ALL
1818474,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.5.1.1.3,1955-07-20,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Mr. Drew:,Leader of the Official Opposition,ATOMIC ENERGY,URANIUM ORE,INQUIRY AS TO PURCHASES BY GOVERNMENT,Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if it is not correct that only within the past few days official statements have been made both in Britain and in the United States that there is a shortage of uranium. I should like to ask him how that conforms with the position now taken that there will be no firm date for the continuing of purchases of uranium here.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Alexander Drew,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce&Language=E&Section=ALL
1818475,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.5.1.1.4,1955-07-20,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. Howe (Port Arthur):,Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce,ATOMIC ENERGY,URANIUM ORE,INQUIRY AS TO PURCHASES BY GOVERNMENT,There never has been a firm date for the purchase of uranium except at the price made public. We have an announced price for uranium. If people can bring a mine into production and sell the product at the price that is underwritten, the product would be accepted. Usually people expect a definite contract for a somewhat better price. Those are worked out individually. I know of no present shortage of uranium. Our production goes up steadily. As I say, I do not think anyone is in a position to say that the government will underwrite all the uranium that can be produced until 1962. The situation is that no government is prepared to underwrite the purchase of uranium produced after 1962. But to say that the government guarantees to purchase all uranium that is produced until 1962 is not correct.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1818476,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.5.1.1.5,1955-07-20,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Mr. Drew:,Leader of the Official Opposition,ATOMIC ENERGY,URANIUM ORE,INQUIRY AS TO PURCHASES BY GOVERNMENT,Mr. Speaker, I have no desire to pursue this unnecessarily beyond the extreme importance of this development. Is it not true that the opinion has been expressed that, with the peacetime developments of the use of uranium, it is unlikely that the supply will keep pace with demand? I asked the question because, even if the government is not prepared to support the statement that has appeared today that they are going to purchase uranium products up to 1962, the knowledge of the decision in that respect will in itself have a substantial bearing on the impetus behind the exploratory work that is being done.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Alexander Drew,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce&Language=E&Section=ALL
1818477,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.5.1.1.6,1955-07-20,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. Howe (Port Arthur):,Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce,ATOMIC ENERGY,URANIUM ORE,INQUIRY AS TO PURCHASES BY GOVERNMENT,Speculating on

the peacetime market for uranium is speculating without any solid basis in fact. I would not care to speculate to that extent. I believe there will be a peacetime market for uranium. At that time the government will not be underwriting purchases. Sales will be a private enterprise transaction. All I can say is that, if anyone wants an answer as to what the government is prepared to do about a particular property, the facts should be presented to Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited and an answer obtained direct. I would not care to give a general statement.
On the orders of the day:

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL

Hodgson (Victoria, Onl.):",,ATOMIC ENERGY,URANIUM ORE,INQUIRY AS TO PURCHASES BY GOVERNMENT,"With respect to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition having to do with uranium, I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to tell us if his department or the government will allow the export of uranium concentrates to the United States and Great Britain.

,Progressive Conservative,,Clayton Wesley Hodgson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=23a7a700-cb63-453a-9f72-9f556f34686c&Language=E&Section=ALL
1818479,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.5.1.1.8,1955-07-20,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. Howe (Port Arthur):,Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce,ATOMIC ENERGY,URANIUM ORE,INQUIRY AS TO PURCHASES BY GOVERNMENT,That again is a question that should be taken up with the atomic energy control board about a certain property. 1818515,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.12.1.1.1,1955-07-20,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,NATIONAL REVENUE,ALLEGED ANOMALOUS,POSITION OF MINISTER,Mr. Speaker, I propose to avail myself of the opportunity that this motion presents under the historic procedure of the house to deal with a subject which we regard as being of major importance and which can only be properly and satisfactorily discussed with a definite motion before the House of Commons.

During the present session, and particularly during the more recent weeks of a fairly lengthy session, there has been considerable discussion about the position of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) in relation to certain disclosures that were made by the minister himself under circumstances which I need not now review. It should be recalled that if the subject has been discussed at some length the responsibility for that discussion rests entirely with the minister, who chose to bring it to public attention by the course that he followed. What became public did disclose the conflict of interests that arose because of the dual role of the Minister of National Revenue. In saying that, I am not suggesting that there has been any way in which the minister has done anything that he feels is contrary to the general welfare of the state. The fact remains, however, that the rules or obligations concerning a minister of the crown have been clearly established over long years, and that it is not only our right but our duty when such circumstances arise to make sure we act as custodians of the established principles of the House of Commons and the government, which is the executive of this parliamentary body. When the subject arose it was stated that we would deal with it at some length when the estimates of the Department of National Revenue came before the committee of the whole house. At that time it seemed that this procedure would be the most satisfactory way of dealing with the subject, a subject, I would repeat, which was raised by the action of the minister and not by the action of any hon. member of this house. Our responsibility was presented to us by that action and a public discussion of what had occurred.

Since we stated that this subject would be dealt with at the time the estimates of the Department of National Revenue were called, answers have been given in response to formal questions placed on the order paper 50433-407J

and oral questions asked before the orders of the day were called. The answers which have been given now make it quite clear that it will be fruitless to seek any further information by questioning when the estimates of the department come before the committee. The minister himself and the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) have left no doubt about the fact that answers to questions concerning the contents of certain papers which were discussed publicly as a result of the actions of the minister will not be given to this house. Therefore, it would merely be a frustrating and useless extension of these questions to pursue them further in that manner.

Another reason why it does not now seem appropriate or practical to raise these questions when the estimates of the Department of National Revenue are called is that the whole subject has now become a very simple but fundamentally important question of principle. In response to my questions in the house, the Prime Minister has informed us that he has ascertained the facts from the Minister of National Revenue, and he will not disclose those facts. It is not necessary for us at this stage to argue as to the proper interpretation of the statutes applying to the records which have been under discussion. We have made it clear that we challenge the statement that those terms of secrecy which are in statutory form do apply to any information which might come to the minister in any other capacity than that of minister of the crown or a member of the House of Commons. I repeat, however, that we need not now argue about the legal interpretation of those statutory provisions.

The Prime Minister has made it clear that he does not propose to give that information. Therefore, no useful purpose will be served by seeking to pursue these questions when the estimates of the Prime Minister are before the committee. The simple but important principle which is now before every hon. member in this house is whether or not we are going to respect the clearly established rule, although it may not be a formal rule of the house or a statutory rule, that there must be no conflict of interest between the private interests and the public duties of a minister of the crown; and, moreover, that there must be no possibility of any appearance of conflict of interest between those private interests and public responsibilities.
Let us be quite certain about one aspect of this discussion. We are not now placing before the house for consideration in any indirect form or by any alternative procedure
Minister of National Revenue

a suggestion already made that, without any regard to the facts, a minister of the crown must hold no directorships. I mention that now so that there may be no confusion in the mind of any hon. member in regard to that aspect of this discussion.

There have been those who have sought the approval of the members of this house for the proposal that no minister of the crown may hold any directorship, whatever the nature of that directorship may be.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Alexander Drew,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
1818517,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.12.1.1.3,1955-07-20,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Mr. Drew:,Leader of the Official Opposition,NATIONAL REVENUE,ALLEGED ANOMALOUS,POSITION OF MINISTER,This subject has beeen placed before the house by the introduction of a measure which would have placed this obligation in statutory form. We have already made it clear that we do not support that blanket proposal. We are not, either directly or indirectly, discussing that in raising the question as we now do. We are placing before the house the established responsibility of the Prime Minister to deal with a question which raises any doubt about the position of a minister of the crown where conflict of this kind appears to be an established fact or an open possibility. There is nothing new in this subject which is now raised. It has been discussed over and over again. It has taken clearer and clearer form as years have gone by.

In the early part of the last century, with short sessions of the House of Commons at Westminster, with very short sessions of the legislative bodies in this country, there was a much more informal relationship between the position of the individual and his responsibilities as a minister of the crown. As the traditions we now accept took clearer and clearer form, with the increasing time demanded of the members of the house and the increasing clarity of the obligations of the ministers themselves, there took shape a code of obligations which have been referred to by succeeding prime ministers at Westminster and here at Ottawa.

At Westminster this subject was discussed by Palmerston many long years ago. It was discussed by Campbell-Bannerman; it was discussed by other prime ministers in the intervening years. Then, it was very sharply defined by Mr. Asquith in 1913. I do not intend to quote at any length the statements he made at that time because they referred to different aspects of the obligations of the ministers of the crown who had associations with corporations, either from the point of view of their executive responsibilities or their trading in the shares of those corporations. I merely wish to quote two statements from the observations made by the Right Hon. Herbert Asquith at that time. He
was referring to this code of obligations, as he described them. This is what he said:
The first and the most obvious is that ministers ought not to enter into any transaction whereby their private pecuniary interests might, even conceivably, come into conflict with their public duty.

Then, having reviewed the broad nature of the different types of activities where there could be a conflict of interest, Mr. Asquith referred again to what he called rules of obligation. He added also that there were in addition to those rules of obligation what he described as rules of prudence which could not be ignored. He pointed out that those rules of prudence had never been formulated in such explicit terms as had the rules of obligation, but he then went on to say this, and I give his exact words:

One of those rules is that in these matters such persons should carefully avoid all transactions which can give colour or countenance to the belief that they are doing anything which the rules of obligation forbid.

The Right Hon. Herbert Asquith at that time, as prime minister of Britain, made it perfectly clear that with the necessity for the position of a minister of the crown to be above reproach in every way, not only must the rules of obligation apply but also the rules of prudence as well, if public confidence was to be retained.

This subject was also dealt with by a former prime minister of Canada, the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. It was under discussion in this house in April, 1922. At that time efforts were being made to have restrictions imposed upon the rights of hon. members to hold directorships. At that time Mr. King discussed various proposals which had been put forward. I should say at this point that he did not subscribe to every detail of the motion as presented but he did of course place before the house certain statements which indicate how firmly these principles have become embedded in the traditions of this House of Commons. I shall quote his words as recorded at page 1099 of Hansard for the year 1922. These are his words:

The fourth attitude is the one which I might describe as the Gladstone-Campbell-Bannerman-Asquith attitude, which has been to adopt, not as a written rule, not as a matter of legislation, but as a matter of unwritten policy, subject always to exceptions where exceptions seem to be justifiable, the attitude that ministers of the crown should not retain directorships. That has been the attitude which has been taken by most of the English Liberal statesmen. That attitude is one on which I shall say a few more words a little later on. It is not, as I have mentioned, the enforcement by resolution of the House of Commons, but rather leaving it to the Prime Minister to exercise his judgment in the formation of his cabinet as to what may be most in the public interest and what is best for the nation under the existing circumstances.
Minister of National Revenue

So much, then, for the attitude which the British House of Commons has taken. I think if we are to follow British practice in any particular, we would be justified also in following British procedure in the manner of putting that practice into play. If we are to make prevail in this country an opinion such as is suggested in the motion of my hon. friend, I think it is much better that it should be left to a prime minister, in consultation with his colleagues, to take the course which the public interest seems to dictate as wisest and best, all circumstances being considered, rather than to tie the hands of a prime minister and to fetter his government by restrictions which do not take account of circumstances which in the public interest should be taken account of.

That is the end of the quotation which I wish to place on the record. It will be recognized that in those words a former Liberal prime minister of Canada emphasized the responsibility of the prime minister to make sure that the government which he had been called upon to form should conform with these unwritten, or in some cases written simply in the form of a statement in the House of Commons, rules of obligation and rules of prudence which have come down to us from years of consideration and debate as to the manner in which the public interest can best be served by members of the House of Commons and members of their executive chosen by the prime minister himself.

This subject came under discussion on later occasions. It came before the House of Commons at Westminster on February 25, 1952. Reference has been made already to the statement made tnen by the prime minister of Great Britain, at that time Right Hon. Winston Churchill. So that the context may be complete I wish to repeat some of the statements made at that time by the prime minister of Great Britain in view of the fact that he himself made it clear that he was merely summing up practices long established. On that occasion, as recorded at page 702 of the British House of Commons Hansard for February 25, 1952, I find a statement by the prime minister of Great Britain. He explained that what he was then placing before the house had been distributed in written form for the guidance of ministers of the crown in regard to this particular subject. This had already been placed before the ministers. It seems to me that the practice established on that occasion by Mr. Churchill was a commendable practice which left no uncertainty as to the attitude of the prime minister of the day in that or in other similar houses of commons in regard to this subject. I now wish to refer to certain paragraphs of this statement circulated among the ministers
of the crown which apply directly to the subject under discussion. They are as follows:

column2: It is a principle of public life that ministers must so order their affairs that no conflict arises, or appears to arise, between their private interests and their public duties.

Such a conflict may arise if a minister takes an active part in any undertaking which may have contractual or other relations with a government department, more particularly with his own department. It may arise, not only if the minister has a financial interest in such an undertaking, but also if he is actively associated with any body, even of a philanthropic character, which might have negotiations or other dealings with the government or be involved in disputes with it. Furthermore ministers should be free to give full attention to their official duties, and they should not engage in other activities which might be thought to distract their attention from those duties.

Each minister must decide for himself how these principles apply to him. Over much of the field, as is shown below, there are established precedents; but in any case of doubt the prime minister of the day must be the final judge, and ministers should submit any such case to him for his direction.

Where it is proper for a minister to retain any private interest, it is the rule that he should declare that interest to his colleagues if they have to discuss public business in any way affecting it, and that he should entirely detach himself from the consideration of that business.
Ministers include all members of the government except unpaid assistant government whips.

column1: Directorships

column2: Ministers must on assuming office resign any directorships which they may hold, whether in public or in private companies and whether the directorship carries remuneration or is honorary. The only exception to this rule is that directorships in private companies established for the maintenance of private family estates, and only incidentally concerned in trading, may be retained subject to this reservation-that if at any time the minister feels that conflict is likely to arise between this private interest and his public duty, he should even in those cases divest himself of his directorship. Directorships or offices held in connection with philanthropic undertakings should also be resigned if there is any risk of conflict arising between the interests of the undertakings and the government.

column1: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to read further from the statement which had been circulated among the ministers of the crown because the subsequent paragraphs refer to shareholdings and speculative activities which do not apply in this particular case. I admit that conceivably they too might apply under certain circumstances.

What is the situation that we have before us? The situation fully disclosed in this house is that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) is a director of the Guaranty Trust Company. Can it be said that this directorship conflicts or could have the appearance of conflicting with his duties as a minister of the crown? I submit that there can be no reasonable doubt that it does.
Let us see exactly what this responsibility entails. There might be many companies where it would be a borderline case, where
Minister of National Revenue

the discussion might be in the twilight zone of uncertainty. That does not apply here. Every trust company in this country has a direct contact with the government but, above all, it has a direct contact with the Department of National Revenue. Even if it could be argued-and I submit the argument could not properly be sustained-that a trust company dealing with some other department of government than that occupied by a minister who is a director would not raise a controversy, it does not apply in this case because the minister is a director of a company which must deal with the very department for which he has administrative responsibilities and wide discretionary powers.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Alexander Drew,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce&Language=E&Section=ALL

1818521,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.12.1.1.7,1955-07-20,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Mr. Drew:,Leader of the Official Opposition,NATIONAL REVENUE,ALLEGED ANOMALOUS,POSITION OF MINISTER,Mr. Speaker, I am dealing with the principle of parliamentary procedure, and my remarks and the motion itself will relate directly to what I believe to be the responsibility of the Prime Minister in relation to the House of Commons itself. In connection with the aspect of the subject I was just discussing, I would point out that there might conceivably be a debate if, merely as an example, the Minister of Fisheries were a director of a trust company which would be dealing with the Department of National Revenue. I do not believe that there should be a debate. I believe that, if the Minister of Fisheries were a director, he should resign from that directorship immediately if that company were dealing with the government.

Under our system the government is one executive. But even if there could be any argument on that score-and may I say I was merely using the name of the Minister of Fisheries as an illustration and not suggesting that he is a director of any company at this time-I would point out that, if such a debate could be sustained, that cannot apply to this case now before us.

Let us see what a trust company must do -any trust company. Let me just illustrate by a few examples. In these days of increasingly complex responsibilities of all individuals who are in business of one kind and another, a practice has developed of making trust companies agents for individuals in the administration of their personal affairs. Any agency of a living person carried on by a trust company would of necessity be dealing day by day, or certainly periodically, with the Department of National Revenue. A trust company would also be dealing with a substantial number of trusteeships where the interests of living people would be affected by the periodic transactions that would take place between that trust company and the Department of National Revenue.

Then let us look at what arises in the case of estates, and let us particularly remember the case of estates. There a trust company must inevitably deal with the Department of National Revenue. There are other illustrations, many of them, that I could offer, where a trust company must periodically and frequently deal with the Department of
Minister of National Revenue

National Revenue. In a very large number of those cases the decisions that will be made by the department are discretionary decisions placed by statute under the minister himself. Therefore you have the extraordinary situation that a minister of the crown is, in an executive capacity as a director, part of the corporate body which is regularly dealing with his own department, and having discretionary decisions made by that minister himself which have a direct bearing upon the transactions with the trust company of which he is an executive member.

There could not conceivably be under any circumstances a more sharply defined example of conflict of interests than that which has been clearly placed before this House of Commons by the statements which have been made here and which were first brought out into the open by the action of the minister himself. The Prime Minister has said that this is a matter of conscience. There must, of course, be cases where the decision will be a matter of conscience. There must, of course, be cases where it will be for the minister to decide whether he is in duty bound to disclose certain facts to the Prime Minister and to his colleagues as to possible conflict of interests. That could arise in the case of some personal activities and personal interests, but this is no such hidden activity. The Minister of National Revenue is shown to the public by the public advertisements and otherwise of the Guaranty Trust Company to be a director of that company and in his executive capacity one who, as part of the corporate body, is dealing with his own department over which he exercises administrative responsibilities as a minister of the crown.

This situation has existed for years. Never has it been brought into such sharp focus as on this occasion when the minister himself has focused attention on that conflict of responsibilities by his own action, which has been fully dealt with in the press and by certain questions already raised in this house.

Mr. Speaker, all Canadians are interested in this subject. All Canadians are interested in income taxes. All Canadians are interested in succession duties if they have any personal holdings of any substantial nature. Income taxes affect most Canadians at this time. Succession duties affect a large percentage of Canadians. As has been shown over and over again, the discretionary powers of the minister with regard to income taxes and succession duties are extremely wide. They are so wide, in fact, that our courts from time to time have seriously questioned the propriety of retaining such extensive discretionary powers. However, I only mention
that point in order to illustrate how real those discretionary powers now are.

How can we as members of this House of Commons, carrying forward traditions which have been mentioned by every prime minister, ignore the responsibilities that have now been imposed upon us by the open discussion throughout Canada of this very subject? I submit that we are the custodians of these great principles and that every hon. member on both sides of this house is bound to examine his own conscience when he deals with this subject and determines the position he will take. In raising this subject I am not suggesting that either party which has had the responsibility of government- and I sometimes think that it may be necessary to repeat that there have been only two parties that have had that responsibility and that there are only two parties that are likely to have it-

1818532,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.12.1.1.18,1955-07-20,ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce,ca.m.5467,Mr. Drew:,Leader of the Official Opposition,NATIONAL REVENUE,ALLEGED ANOMALOUS,POSITION OF MINISTER,Mr. Speaker, I suggest that it has been made perfectly clear that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself must assume the responsibility. The Prime Minister himself is the individual who has been entrusted by the crown with the responsibility for forming a government in the first instance. With that obligation clearly stated, I think that once there is any uncertainty, we should go back to the many occasions when it has been pointed out that the Prime Minister himself must decide what should be done. Since the Minister of National Revenue has not seen fit to draw a distinction between his position as a private citizen and as a minister of the crown and between the personal interests and public responsibilities which come into conflict on this occasion so sharply and so clearly, then I submit that the Prime Minister himself unquestionably must exercise that responsibility.

Simply because it is the most recent summing up of those rules of conduct, of those rules of obligation and of prudence and not simply because it was stated in Westminster or stated by Sir Winston Churchill, I would point out once again what he said on that occasion. In summing up the principles and traditions of many long years of parliamentary practice which we accept, he said that it is for each minister to decide for himself how these principles apply to him. But then he went on and said this:
. . . but in any case of doubt the prime minister of the day must be the final judge, . . .

That is clear enough. That is definite enough. Surely there can be no doubt about it that since the Prime Minister accepts the responsibility of forming the government, he continues to be responsible for the conduct of the whole government. Therefore if there is a conflict of interest, it is for the Prime Minister to deal with it.

It is not something that any of us likes to raise here when any individual is concerned. We have no desire to deal with an individual as an individual. We are dealing with the position of the Minister of National Revenue within a Canadian government under long-established and extremely important principles. Anything that is said or anything that has been said would apply with equal force to any minister of any department. This is no borderline case. This is no twilight zone of uncertainty. There is no doubt here. There is a conflict of interests where a minister of

the crown in his private capacity is part of a corporate body which deals periodically with the department of which that same minister is the administrative head, with infinitely wide powers of discretion which could be exercised to the advantage of the corporate body of which he is an executive member. There could not be a sharper or clearer conflict of interest than there is in this case.

Let no one suggest, in answer to this statement, that there has been no evidence that any advantage has been taken of this conflict of interest. Let no one suggest that no evidence has been offered that any pecuniary advantage has accrued to the minister. We are not suggesting that. We say that the rules of conduct are clear. There must not only be an absence of conflict of interest but there must be no appearance to the public that there could be any conflict of interest.

We believe that the time is overdue for the Prime Minister to act with regard to this clearly-established conflict of interest. It is something that relates to no individual but to the principles of government inherent in our parliamentary system. There are two choices open. They apply to any person, no matter who that person may be. The Prime Minister should either call upon the minister to resign his directorship or he should call upon him to resign as a minister of the crown. It could be nothing less. No other course can dispose of this conflict.

I therefore place before this house a resolution which leaves the responsibility with the Prime Minister, which does not seek to tie his hands, but which simply seeks to have the members of the house indicate that they wish the Prime Minister to accept his responsibility under the long-established rules of conduct which have come down to us over many generations of parliamentary history. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton):
That all the words after ""That"" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
in the opinion of this house the Prime Minister should take appropriate action with respect to the conflict between the private interests and public duties of the Minister of National Revenue.""

I may be completely wrong and therefore will not make a ruling until I have checked the authorities, but I should like to make certain observations. The first one is that the amendment is a vote of want of confidence. It states that the Prime Minister should take appropriate action with respect to the conflict between private interests and public duties. It states that there is a conflict between the private
Minister of National Revenue

interests and public duties of the Minister of National Revenue. It seems to me that this implies a charge against the Minister of National Revenue which could be more appropriately dealt with by a substantive motion. That is my first observation.

My second observation is the following. In dealing with the amendment to the motion to go into supply, citation 467 of Beau-chesne, third edition, reads in part as follows: When such motion is proposed, it shall be permissible to discuss any public matter within the powers of the federal parliament-
Within the powers of the federal parliament"".
-or to ask for the redress of any grievance, and it is not necessary to move an amendment for that purpose . . .

May I now refer to the debate that took place on the motion for second reading of Bill No. 379, moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, which bill is still on the order paper, and to which motion an amendment was moved by the Minister of Finance. The main amending section of the bill to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act reads as follows:

No person who is a director of a company incorporated under the Companies Act or under any other public general act of Canada, or incorporated by a local or private act of Canada, shall be eligible to be a member of the Queen's privy council for Canada and a minister of the crown.

If this matter were to be decided in the affirmative by the house surely the amendment proposed today would not be necessary. As far as the rules of debate are concerned, there is certainly a conflict between Bill No. 379, which is still on the order paper and may well come up for discussion, and the amendment now proposed which deals substantially with the same subject matter. I come back to the point that I made a moment ago with respect to citation 467, and in the course of the debate on Bill No. 379 I see that the Leader of the Opposition said, as found at page 4509:

Under our system the Prime Minister is called upon by the representative of the Queen, or of the King as the case may be, to form a government. The ministers are not chosen by the crown; the Prime Minister is asked to form a government.
As found at page 4510 he also had this to say regarding the rules with respect to the clarification of situations such as the one contemplated by the motion:
These rules have been established for some time. He was referring to the rules laid down by Mr. Asquith and former prime minister Churchill. He went on to say:
They must be established by the Prime Minister, because he accepts the responsibility from the crown.

Is not the house at the moment asking the Prime Minister to establish something which it is his prerogative to establish? Would the house, for instance, dictate, by way of amendment to the motion to go into supply, how the Prime Minister is going to appoint senators? Under our system the Prime Minister is invested with certain prerogatives which are age-old and which, as I often heard said in the house, are derived from the crown. It is true that at one time they were held by the crown, but these residual prerogatives are now held by the Prime Minister and his colleagues.

In making these observations I may, as I said, be completely wrong. I take it the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe must think I am wrong, but I should like to check the authorities. I did not wish hon. members to be caught by surprise if I should come to the conclusion, and I hope to reach a conclusion as soon as possible, that the amendment is not in order, and I wanted them to have a preview of how my thinking goes at the moment.

St. Laurent (Prime Minister):,Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council,NATIONAL REVENUE,ALLEGED ANOMALOUS,POSITION OF MINISTER,I hope I will have an opportunity of making a few observations in answer to the speech of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) before you make a ruling that would prevent anything further from being said upon the matter. There is not very much that I feel it is necessary to say. I am sorry this question arises at a time when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) is not in his seat. He felt it was his duty, as the minister reporting to parliament with respect to matters concerning the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to attend the funeral of a distinguished member of the board of that corporation which is taking place in Montreal this morning, a gentleman who had been associated with the minister in the administration of the affairs of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for many years and who had rendered in that capacity important services to the people of Canada.

Now, that being said I wish to deal with some of the matters that have been dealt with by the Leader of the Opposition. First of all, I will say to him that I will never shirk any responsibility for the propriety of the conduct of any member of the government while he remains a member of the government. I realize fully that responsibility, and I intend to discharge that responsibility fully. I am confident that I have fully discharged that responsibility. When I had the honour of being called upon to form a government, there was a government in office that had received many testimonials of the confidence of the Canadian public. Most of the members of that government did me the honour of agreeing to serve with me as they had served with my predecessor. I knew at that time
Minister of National Revenue

that the Minister of National Revenue had been told what the leader of that government had told me when he did me the honour of inviting me to become associated with him: that is to say, it was my responsibility to decide whether or not I should sever all connections with business corporations with which I had been associated before I received his invitation. He had told the Minister of National Revenue the same thing, and the minister had felt there was not going to be any possibility of or appearance of possible conflict between his private interests and his duty to the Canadian public. I had felt that there would have been no possibility of conflict of interest in the way I discharged my duties as minister, when I became one, and those other connections, but I did not want to be exposed to any unfair criticism, which is unfortunately frequently the lot of those who do attempt to serve their fellow citizens in public life.

Now, that was the situation when I became leader of a government in which the present Minister of National Revenue was the Minister of National Revenue. I have ascertained that there has never been any conflict of interest between the private interests of the Minister of National Revenue and his responsibilities in his official capacity. There did arise an incident that has brought about this discussion. When we had the federal-provincial conference here last April the provincial treasurer of the province of Ontario, who is the premier of that province, was here. He had some of his officials with him. I heard afterwards that the Minister of National Revenue had in his possession photostatic copies of certain receipts, one of which implied that a certain sum of money had been handed to the gentleman who signed the receipt for the purpose of acquiring for the deceased person Drohan an asset in the form of an interest in forest lands under the control of the Ontario government. I was told that the Minister of National Revenue came down in the afternoon intending to show this receipt to Mr. Chester Walters, the controller of the department of finance there, and to inquire from him whether there was anything in their records that would show an asset corresponding to the terms of this receipt had been acquired, because there was nothing in the assets that had been declared by the estate that seemed to correspond with such assets as might have been acquired or should have been acquired with the proceeds in respect of which that receipt had been issued.
Mr. Walters had left for Toronto on the afternoon train, so the Minister of National Revenue showed the receipt and made the same inquiry from the provincial treasurer 50433-408i

of Ontario, who happens to be the premier of Ontario. Now, that was all that was done by the Minister of National Revenue. Subsequently, the man who had signed the receipt appears to have made a statement to the press that he had an interview with the premier of Ontario who told him that until this matter was cleared up, as well as other matters connected with moneys for which there were other receipts, he would not have the support of the Progressive Conservative party in the provincial election that was then going to take place. The publicity that came about this came from the statements made by Mr. Dempsey.

There was a question put by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy), following an article or an editorial that appeared in the Globe and Mail, and that was on May 9, 1955. In answer to that question put by the hon. member for York South, the Minister of National Revenue made the answers which appear in Hansard for May 9, 1955, at page 3565. I will not take the time of the house to read the answers that were given on that occasion, but the minister did say:

Under section 133 of the Income Tax Act and section 55 of the succession duty act, I must observe the secrecy provisions of those acts and not disclose to anyone not entitled to know any matter concerning any estate in question. The estate in question involved both income tax and succession duties. The Ontario provincial treasurer, Premier Frost, is entitled to any information the Department of National Revenue has with reference to succession duties. Interchange of information is a common practice. I admit that I had a conference with Mr. Frost while he was in Ottawa. He had to leave hurriedly, so that the conference was incomplete. I am not in a position to disclose any information that passed between us at that time.

That is the origin of the publicity that was attached to this incident during the course of the recent provincial election in Ontario. Now, that is all that took place and that is the only way in which the minister was by his conduct, as stated by the Leader of the Opposition, responsible for the publicity. The publicity did not come from the minister. The publicity came from the man who had signed the receipt, and the further publicity which came from the minister was in answer to a question asked of him in the house by the hon. member for York South before the orders of the day were called. I was asked myself afterwards whether I would ascertain what the facts were and satisfy myself that there had been no wrongdoing. I did so, and so declared in the house on a subsequent date. The date itself is not important. I declared in the house that I had satisfied myself there had been nothing wrong done. I repeated to the Minister of National Revenue that it was for each one of us,
Minister of National Revenue
according to the traditions that had been maintained up to that time, to decide whether or not he should sever his connections with any corporation with which he had had or did have connections.

There was one other occasion when I was asked whether I did not find that there was some conflict there that was undesirable. I said that I had ascertained there had been nothing that affected my confidence in the Minister of National Revenue in the faithful performance of his duties to the Canadian public, as I know he has been performing them during those many years. More recently some other questions were raised at the time answers were given to questions that were placed on the order paper. The Minister of National Revenue then informed me that on June 20 he had resigned his directorship with the Guaranty Trust Company, and that he had done so not that he felt there was anything wrong in his being associated with it, but that he felt there were a large number of members in the House of Commons who felt it undesirable that he should continue to be a director of the Guaranty Trust Company, and that out of his respect for the feeling of members of the House of Commons, that he personally did not share, he had informed his co-directors that he was resigning his office. He told me that was done on June 20. I did express to him my admiration of the fact that, though he did not share the views of those members of the House of Commons whose respect he wanted to retain, out of respect for their views he had taken that course of action. I am sorry he is not here himself to make a fuller statement in that respect.

There has been no clash of private interest with the discharge of public responsibilities. There were placed on the record here on June 7, by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), those rules which the Leader of the Opposition read again today into the record. One of them is, or was, in the opinion of Mr. Churchill, that each minister must decide for himself how those principles apply to him. Well, the Minister of National Revenue did decide for himself how those principles applied to him. He had no doubt about it, and there was no doubt expressed to me, and I had no doubt that, though I would not have wished to incur the unfair criticism that has been heaped upon the Minister of National Revenue, he was faithfully discharging his duties as a minister of the crown.
I had no hesitation as Prime Minister of the government in which he is a minister in having my part of that responsibility, because
I was perfectly satisfied that his responsibilities were being discharged not only in an honest, but in an efficient, manner.

The motion that the Leader of the Opposition submits does imply that there was a conflict between the private interests and the public duties of the Minister of National Revenue. As far as I am concerned I am satisfied that there was none, and I am satisfied that the responsibilities of my oath of office and my desire to serve efficiently my fellow citizens are being discharged in an efficient manner, too. I had no feeling that would have required me to take any action.

If there is any desire on the part of anyone-call it a charge, call it a suggestion, or call it whatever he likes-to put to a vote of this house something which implies wrongdoing on the part of the Minister of National Revenue, I think Your Honour is apt to come to the conclusion that that is something which would have to be done by motion in which notice was given in the manner required by the rules and could not be brought on incidentally as a grievance on a motion to go into committee of supply.

1818594,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.13.1.2,1955-07-20,7f8b0a5f-7e1a-49b0-8f27-209db21f611a,ca.m.8094,Mr. J. Wilfrid Dufresne (Quebec Wesl):,,POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT,ALLEGED THEFTS,,Mr. Speaker, for some years now large thefts have occurred in many Canadian post offices, notably in Montreal and suburbs. With a few rare exceptions, investigations of those thefts have led to no positive results, and the largest of such thefts, i.e. those where the guilty parties secured large amounts of money, have not yet been cleared up. In spite of the so-called investigations we heard so much about, the thieves are still at large and their spoils remain undiscovered.

Several times in the past I have attempted to bring to the acting minister's attention the serious irregularities which have been rife in his department. More particularly, I have put several questions to him recently, which should have aroused his attention and suspicion.

In spite of the fact that the public had been thoroughly aroused and were expecting a serious and exhaustive investigation of this abnormal and intolerable state of affairs, it has been learned, with considerable surprise, that certain Post Office Department employees, who had much to do with those investigations, had been promoted instead of being questioned.

Last year, the deputy postmaster general. Mr. Walter J. Turnbull, the acknowledged head of the department which he administers with a velvet-gloved iron hand, put in charge of those investigations a certain party from whom the public was entitled to expect results. However, from the time that appointment was made, the thieves, past-masters in the art of looting post offices, have carried their operations to such a pitch that the Canadian people, in terror, have been asking when the departmental authorities would carry out appropriate measures to put an end to these unpunished crimes against the government.

Acting under mounting public pressure, the deputy postmaster general, Mr. Turnbull, communicated to his postmasters and to the press additional directives concerning steps to be taken to protect public funds and to put an end to the activity of those unsatiable thieves. On December 15, every newspaper carried the following announcement:
Ottawa Warns Postmasters

Ottawa, December 15. (BUP)-The Post Office Department today informed all postmasters across the country of the growing number of post office robberies. All postmasters have been warned to take all possible precautions to insure the pro-
tection of postal values (stamps, money orders, etc.) and to adhere strictly to the rules governing this matter.
So stated the notice signed by Mr. W. J. Turnbull, deputy postmaster general.

Special attention must be given to the rule requiring postmasters to dispose of all cash exceeding the amount of their authorized reserves, and to keep accurate lists of money orders and bills kept overnight.

It seems to me that this warning should have served as an ultimatum to those who are in charge of investigations and should have prompted them to unmask the really responsible ones, and to bring them before criminal courts.

Not only was there a failure to bring before the courts individuals whose participation in very large robberies had been established, but, with the collusion of certain investigators, these crooks were secreted from justice, and the Post Office Department itself paid for having them put away at the proper time and place so they would not be troubled.

On several occasions and in various clubs and taverns of the city of Montreal, a notorious criminal could be seen for hours on end drinking with some investigators, giving the impression that they were settling personal matters of great import.

On September 17, 1954, less than a year ago, an investigator went to Seven Islands, Quebec, in company with a man who was more than once involved in post office robberies, for the purpose of finding him employment as a labourer with the Iron Ore Company of Canada.
For reasons which cannot be commendable, but rather blameworthy, this individual, called Marcel Belair, had to be taken away for the obvious purpose of hiding him from justice.
So the trip was made by air from Quebec to Seven Islands. The two men stayed at the local hotel for three days under aliases, and the Post Office Department footed the bill.

The Post Office Department investigator called on the manager of the Iron Ore Company of Canada, who happens to be the mayor of Seven Islands, in an attempt to induce him to co-operate with the department in giving Marcel Belair a job as a labourer under the name of Arthur St. Jean. The investigator undertook, on behalf of the department, to assure the manager that he would take responsibility for any false papers that would be issued. An identification card was also issued by the unemployment insurance commission office through
Post Office Department
the same means and again under the name of Arthur St. Jean, who was none other than Marcel Belair.

The department, through its acting minister, confirmed what I have just said in answering certain questions I asked recently. The answer to these questions are to be found at page 4980 of Hansard for June 20 of this year.

At a time when unemployment had already made its dismal appearance in Seven Islands district and hundreds of family heads were looking for work, the Post Office Department, through its investigators and under the high protection and direction of the deputy minister, was compelling the Iron Ore Company of Canada to give employment to a post office thief at large, and having false papers issued to that individual, who did not want to work, as evidenced by the fact that, as soon as the investigators had left Seven Islands, Belair likewise left, for Montreal. Therefore I say that the Post Office Department, and its investigator under its instructions, are guilty of forgery, which is an indictable offence under sections 466 and 467 of our Criminal Code and, as such, liable to a prison term.

Mr. Speaker, in the fall of 1953, a large theft took place at the post office of Cabano, a village in Temiscouata county, in the province of Quebec. About three months later, i.e., on January 15, 1954, two individuals were brought before the court at Riviere du Loup, under a charge of receiving and concealing, to which they pleaded guilty. One of them was sentenced to a two-year term in a penitentiary, whereas the other, who had co-operated by writing out a confession under oath, only got three months' imprisonment.

A third man had, however, also been questioned with regard to this theft; he was none other than Marcel Belair who was, like the rest of the gang, identified by several people before and after the theft, when he was keeping company with the other two who were arrested and sentenced. Belair never was troubled by the police, though in the written confession made under oath by one of the accused men, the latter did not fail formally to implicate Belair in the theft.

Why was Belair not arrested right then and brought before the court, as his part in this criminal action was known? This was nothing but an attempt to interfere with justice and, consequently, it is a criminal act punishable by imprisonment. And how is it that at the time of the arrest of the two men who were later found guilty of receiving and concealing in connection with the Cabano robbery, and later on also, a certain post

office investigator had several meetings alone with Belair during which they consumed alcoholic beverages in a hotel in the east end of Montreal, and some other shady spots of the metropolis?

Mr. Speaker, I was very much amused to hear the Acting Postmaster General tell us, or rather tell my hon. colleague from Notre Dame de Grace (Mr. Hamilton), that the post office had no police of its own.

That statement, in my opinion, is most ludicrous. Everybody in this house, as well as a good section of the people, are aware that post office investigators are peace officers, as defined in our Criminal Code, and most of them are justices of the peace. That confers upon them the power to arrest on the spot, without a warrant, any person suspected of committing an indictable offence. Arrest even on warrant is ordinarily vested with the provincial police of each province, due to the fact that the administration of justice is the responsibility of the provinces under the British North America Act, but complaints are generally signed by the post office investigators.

The post office investigators make up the secret police of that department and consequently they do not go about with a club in their hands or wearing a brass-buttoned tunic. However they proceed in the same way and possess the same prerogatives as detectives on various police forces. Therefore, post office investigators, together with Turnbull as their chief, make up the Post Office Department police force. Not only is there nothing wrong with that, but I submit it is a necessity.
It is a recognized fact that the post office has an open account in all courts of justice in Canada; and that its investigators make use of it when they need to.

On February 20, 1954, a theft of $29,142.99 took place at the Notre Dame de Grace post office, in the city of Montreal. The post office investigators reported on the theft to the local police which launched an investigation.

About a week later, the post office investigators learned that their friend Marcel Belair was in possession of $28,000 worth of stamps stolen at Notre Dame de Grace. Zaplitny (Dauphin):,,DISABLED PERSONS ACT-REGULATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, the subject matter about which I wish to speak does not follow the topic which has just been discussed so if there is any hon. member who wishes to discuss that topic I am ready to give him the floor. If not, I shall proceed. The matter to which I wish to direct the attention of the house and which I consider to be of considerable urgency to a number of Canadians, which in fact is a matter of concern to all Canadians, is the question of the regulations under the Disabled Persons Act. I know that a few days ago the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) drew the attention of the Minister of National IMr. Dufresne.]

Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) to the complete inadequacy of the regulations as they now stand, but he received no assurance either then or previously when he had raised the question that anything would be done about this matter before the next session of parliament.

I am sure that the experience of most if not all hon. members of this house who have attempted to be of assistance to their constituents who are unfortunate enough to have to apply for the disability allowance has been most disappointing. It certainly has been in my own experience and that of my colleagues. As a matter of fact the general opinion today-this is substantiated by doctors with whom I have spoken-is that the regulations as they now stand are scandalously stingy and that the way in which they operate makes a complete mockery of the intent and purpose of the act as it was passed in this house. This is a matter of urgency because there are thousands of people across this country, perhaps the most unfortunate individuals in our society, who have made application for this disability allowance but who have been turned down. Large numbers more will be turned down unless the regulations are made more lenient.

As the minister has pointed out, these regulations were drawn up in co-operation with the provinces. There is to be a dominion-provincial conference in this city, I understand, in October and I submit that it is the duty of the minister of health and welfare to take the initiative in discussing these regulations with the representatives of the provinces not later than this fall with a view to bringing about a new definition of the term ""total and permanent disability"".

The way in which that term is being interpreted at this time-I do not intend to go into detail-is almost equal to saying that if a person still breathes he is considered to be not disabled. Some cases I have seen and some cases that have been recounted to me by my colleagues and others reflect a most scandalous situation. Persons who have absolutely no hope of earning a living for themselves, either now or in the future, are told that because they are able to move about and dress themselves and feed themselves they are not considered totally disabled.

Surely a country which boasts of its great prosperity is not going to be so stingy as to say to our disabled persons, ""As long as you can move about, as long as you can dress yourself, as long as you can feed yourself, even if you have nothing with which to feed yourself or nothing with which to dress yourself, you are not a disabled person and we
Disabled Persons Act

take no responsibility for you under this act."" Surely this parliament when it passed the Disabled Persons Act did not intend that it should be administered in that parsimonious, stingy and callous manner. I think it is time that the government took note of this and took some immediate action together with the provinces to see that those who are now waiting for even the small amount which is offered to them under the act may have the benefit of that little bit instead of having to sit around and wait and wade through miles of red tape and tons of correspondence before their cases can be brought before a board.

There is another section of the act which is sorely in need of amendment and this is another subject which probably could be taken up with the provinces at the same time. I refer to that section which denies any assistance to a disabled person who is in an institution or a nursing home. I have received, as I know other hon. members have, resolutions and protests from municipalities which are now charged with the responsibility of caring for such persons. I am sure that all hon. members know that so far as public institutions and nursing homes are concerned they are carried on as charitable institutions. I cannot think of any public institution which is taking care of disabled or aged persons that is doing so at a profit.

Every such institution is being subsidized in one way or another, either by charitable donations, or if it is operated by church authorities the employees donate their time. In our town there is an institution which takes care of the aged that is run by the nursing sisters. If they were not donating their time or if they were being paid even the minimum wage of our province that institution would not be able to operate. They must carry on with donations from interested citizens and donate their time and services in order to keep it going. But if a disabled person happens to be in such institution and applies for assistance under the act, at the present time he is denied that assistance.

That part of the act must be changed and the regulations must be relaxed if we are going to be able to say that we have passed an act to help to look after disabled persons in this country and that we meant what we said when we passed such act. When we consider the number who have applied in good faith for assistance and the small number that have been granted assistance, it represents a scandalous situation. I think it is a shame that we should be expected to stand for such a condition much longer.
According to the bureau of statistics the liquor bill in Canada last year amounted to

$724 million, or almost three-quarters of a billion dollars. This was more than the total Canadian budget in pre-war years including national defence. If we add the expenditures on tobacco and recreation we have a total of over $1,000 million. A country that can spend over $1,000 million on such things as liquor and tobacco and sometimes very questionable recreation certainly should be able to provide for those unfortunates who have the right to live and to receive some of the good things that are produced in such abundance in this country. If we are willing to spend three-quarters of a billion dollars on liquor-I am not objecting to anyone consuming liquor if he feels so inclined, as that is his business-then we should be able to provide this paltry assistance to those who require it.

When one looks over the correspondence that goes back and forth between the applicant and the provincial board administering the act it unfolds a sad tale. These people are told that the members of the board are manacled by the regulations, that their hands are tied. These boards are made up of sympathetic people who would like to do something. I have discussed this matter privately with some of them and I find them to be dissatisfied at having to administer an act under regulations which to them represent a callous disregard for human welfare. Yet what can we do? It is time that this government through the Minister of National Health and Welfare, took the initiative together with the provinces this fall, and no later than this fall, and brought in a set of regulations more humane and more in line with the intention of this parliament when the act was passed.

Noseworthy (York South):,,DISABLED PERSONS ACT-REGULATIONS,,,Mr. Speaker, the member who has just taken his seat stated that we have not yet had enough time or experience with this act to know just what amendments should be made. The regulations pertaining to this particular act follow closely the regulations that were in effect regarding a similar act in the province of Ontario, administered by the Conservative government of that province. I want to say that the Liberal government should have known better than to have imitated anything that that Conservative government of Ontario is doing, when it came to the administering of an act of this kind.

Before the act was introduced, I called the attention of the house to a situation exactly similar to that which has been raised today. Disabled persons in the province of Ontario, and in the city of Toronto, are unable to get assistance under the provincial act so long as they can shuffle from the bedroom to the kitchen or dining room in their homes. I had cases in Ontario, which I took up with the department, of disabled people who doctors had agreed were permanently disabled and for whom there is no hope. Some of them have not worked for years and have not been able to earn anything for years.

The contention was that, because they could dress themselves and because they could manage to shuffle from the bedroom to other rooms of the house, they were not totally disabled. They must be totally disabled before they could receive help in Ontario. The federal government, in accepting and agreeing to regulations and to a definition of permanent and total disability such as was in effect in Ontario before the federal act was passed, is making a great mistake.

Marler (Minister of Transport):,Minister of Transport,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Mr. Chairman, I intend to follow the practice of my predecessor and to make a statement about the proposed expenditures of my department but because of the stage which the session has reached I shall try to be as brief as circumstances permit.

I do not intend to make a comparison of this year's estimates with those of last year. Instead I shall try to give some information of a general character which will not be found in the details of the estimates themselves.

I should like to deal first with the departmental staff. The establishment for the current fiscal year is to be 11,523 compared to 11,402 last year. This year's figure, of course, does not include 175 departmental personnel who were transferred to the St. Lawrence seaway authority last year and, therefore, are no longer included in the departmental establishment. We consider, however, that we have been fortunate to limit the over-all increase to 121 in the face of the demands for increased services that we have had to meet.

Normal departmental expansion and the introduction of the 40-hour week account for an increase of 53 positions. The shorter work week has not simplified our problems, particularly in posts where operations have to be maintained for 24 hours a day and for 7 days a week, as is the case with our government ships, radio aids to aviation and shipping, weather services, air traffic control, et cetera.

The growth of civil and military flying and our activities in connection with the mid-Canada warning line and distant early warning line have also made it necessary to increase our staff. We have had to provide more than 100 additional positions in air traffic control, 88 for radio aviation, particularly in the north, and more than 50 in meteorology. Moreover, in connection with the sea-lift for the mid-Canada warning line it has been necessary to employ additional seamen, barge operators, and other employees in marine positions who will be engaged for the most part in seasonal work.

I should now like to turn to the construction or acquisition of buildings and works, including land, for which we expect to spend about $35 million. For these purposes the canals branch proposes to make expenditures of

about $2,425,000-about the same as last year-but no major project is involved. Though it is not our policy to effect major expenditures on the St. Lawrence river canals, unless they will be of benefit after the seaway is opened, we are proposing to spend approximately $150,000 for certain works in the Galop canal. Normally this canal is used only for up-bound navigation, but the building of the control dam at Iroquois will necessitate the use of the Galop canal for two-way navigation, and the provision of additional facilities. Our proposed expenditure will be recoverable from the power entities.

As in former years the marine services branch will be carrying out certain essential works for shipping to a total of $1,712,000. The more important projects are: The light station for White island, P.Q., which was not completed last year and for which it is necessary to revote $321,000; the light and fog alarm station at Sand Heads, B.C., to replace a 75-year-old lightship, and a similar station at Cape Scott, B.C., needed because of increased traffic to Kitimat. The cost of these two stations is likely to be about $400,000, of which $290,000 will be spent in the current year.

The main estimates include $1,782,000 for the completion of the program initiated in 1952 for dredging the St. Lawrence ship channel. We expect this program to be finished by mid-summer, but because men and equipment would otherwise remain idle we have provided in supplementary estimates an additional sum of $1,500,000 for further dredging to be done during the balance of the current season. This is a first step towards the additional dredging required to ensure that the channel will be adequate for the increased volume of traffic that may be expected when the seaway has been opened.
A sum of $3,564,000 is required to complete the Canso causeway. The formal opening of this vital link between Cape Breton island and the mainland will take place on August

column2: I am delighted to say that my colleague the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has very kindly agreed to officiate at the ceremonies to be held in this connection.

column1: I have already referred to the growth of civil and military flying. In order that we may continue to maintain the highest safety standards, we propose during the present fiscal year to provide further radio aids to flying and for this purpose to spend some $3J million. We plan to complete the installation of visual omni ranges-VOR-on the airway between Montreal and Windsor and to begin the installation of a similar system on the airway between Toronto and

Winnipeg. We shall also complete the installation at Gander of ground control approach-GCA- for bad weather landings. We expect also to build at Gander a new transmitter station to cost over $300,000 as the existing facilities are now too cramped and must be enlarged. In co-operation with the R.C.A.F. we shall also initiate work at Churchill on new radio facilities to meet the growing need for communications in the north.

We plan to place this year substantial orders for equipment to be delivered in 1956, 1957 and 1958. We propose to purchase visual omni ranges in order to complete the installation on the remaining segments of the transcontinental airway, as well as special surveillance radar sets to provide better air traffic control in the vicinity of our major airports. We also plan, so far as airports are concerned, to continue our program of expanding runways and taxi ways and of installing more and improved lighting systems, particularly high intensity lighting.

We propose to spend substantial sums for the initial stages of a number of terminal buildings. We expect to begin construction at Gander of a new terminal which it is expected will be completed in about a year and a half. We are about to start work on the new terminal at Dorval. This building will not be completed before the latter part of 1957, but it will be a fine, commodious and modern structure and will lend itself to enlargement when greater traffic makes this desirable. Planning on a new terminal for Ottawa is well advanced, and we hope that by mid-autumn we shall begin construction of terminal buildings at the Quebec and Windsor airports.

We have had discussions with the civic authorities in Toronto concerning the Malton airport and the island airport and we believe that at an early date the obstacles to the further development of Malton airport will be removed. As soon as this has been accomplished we propose to make a start on the planning of new terminal facilities, but as it will be some time before the new terminal can be designed and built we are planning some temporary improvements to alleviate congestion in the present building. Plans for new buildings at Winnipeg and Regina are also progressing, although we do not propose to commence construction at either of these places this year.

As part of our plans to keep our airports up to date we shall also be doing work in constructing runways, taxi ways and parking aprons at numerous points, such as Charlottetown, Fredericton, Timmins, Toronto, London, Winnipeg, Yorkton, Calgary, Vancouver and

Yellowknife. We also hope to begin clearing of land at Halifax and Aklavik. Our departmental staff is at present engaged in examining various sites in order to establish a new airport at Edmonton. I think it is important to note in connection with these projects that we are attempting to provide for an increased volume of winter employment. Though much of the work in airport construction can be carried on only during the temperate seasons the construction of buildings and runways and the clearing of land can in certain areas go forward during the winter. Therefore we are attempting to arrange our program so that wherever possible we shall provide some employment during the winter months.
