Mr. Chairman, this concludes my general remarks upon the estimates of my department, but before I resume my seat I think I should deal with one particular subject, that is the vessel William Carson and the harbour of Port aux Basques. A number of
Supply-Transport
questions have been raised in the newspapers and by hon. members, and I believe I should deal with them in order to set the record straight.

The principal criticism is that the water is not deep enough for the William Carson to get into Port aux Basques; that the channel is two feet too shallow to allow the ferry to enter the harbour; and that it will require two years in order to do the necessary dredging.

The fact of the matter is that the channel which has been dredged between Vardy's island and Pike's island has a minimum depth of 23 feet at lowest water spring tide, but for the most part the depth is much greater than 23 feet and in parts it is as great as 50 feet, whereas the draft of the Carson fully loaded is only 19 feet, 3 inches. The dredging carried out was quite sufficient and we have not been considering further dredging of this channel.

While I am on this aspect of the matter, I wish to say that the dredging was done, as was said by my colleague the Minister of Public Works, at a cost of $280,548 and not the $1 million stated in some newspaper reports. The channel to which I have just referred lies almost directly to the south of the terminal wharf from and to which the William Carson is to operate, and provides a straight run into and out from the terminal. It was completed last summer, and the harbour has been under observation since the dredging was finished. The management of the Canadian National Railways, who are to operate the ferry on behalf of the government and who are in consequence to be responsible for the safety of the vessel, recently expressed some fears as to whether wind and wave action would expose the Carson to damage if bad weather conditions developed while she was moored at the terminal and thus make it impossible to maintain uninterrupted service under all weather conditions.

It has been suggested that the effect of wind and wave action could easily have been foreseen, and that what is feared may arise is attributable to the removal of the shoals that formerly afforded protection. Of course, we all know how easy it is to be wise after the event, but in appreciating the validity of these criticisms one must bear in mind two facts. The first is that only a very small portion of the harbour shoals were removed; that these portions were 10 feet or more below the surface of the water and that nearly the whole of these shoals and the whole of Vardy's and Pike's islands still remain. The second is that the new terminal is located upon a site not previously used as

a wharf and there was no earlier experience that would serve to establish what effect wind and wave used to have on that part of the harbour. In these circumstances I do not believe that it can justly be said that the channel that was dredged was wrongly located, or that the wind and wave action that has given rise to the fears of the Canadian National management is the result of the dredging and could have been foreseen when the terminals were built and the dredging of the channel was carried out.

I think I should tell hon. members that there are competent engineers who believe that the effect of wind and wave has been exaggerated, and that the Carson can safely be operated to Port aux Basques as conditions now are, except in unusually bad weather. On the other hand, it must not be overlooked that the Canadian National Railways are to be entrusted with the ship, and it is only reasonable that the doubts that exist in the minds of their responsible officials must be set at rest. Accordingly, after consultation with Mr. Gordon of the Canadian National and my colleague the Minister of Public Works, I have taken steps to obtain a competent independent expert to advise the government as to the present condition of the harbour at Port aux Basques and as to the nature of the further works, if any, that should be undertaken. I am hopeful it will be possible to secure the services of someone who will be able to deal with the matter at once, so that if further works are necessary they may be commenced without delay.

I realize, of course, that it is quite unnecessary to remind hon. members that, under the terms of union with Newfoundland, the service has to be operated between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, so that Canada is committed to carry out at Port aux Basques the works that are necessary to afford safe conditions for the operation of the ferry, regardless of whatever natural difficulties it may be necessary to overcome. But hon. members may not realize that we are also obligated to provide, and I quote the terms of union:
. . . freight and passenger steamship service which, on completion of a motor highway between Corner Brook and Port aux Basques, will include suitable provision for the carriage of motor vehicles.

May I add, in passing, that the motor highway has not yet been completed. But the point I wish to emphasize is that the requirement of a vessel to carry passengers, freight and motor vehicles and the need to maintain the service during the winter months particularly made it essential to build a large ship having sufficient power to operate in ice
Supply-Transport

conditions and at the same time to carry a substantial load. Moreover, the distance to be covered made it necessary that the ship be capable of a reasonably high speed, and be so designed as to allow rapid and efficient loading and unloading. These considerations, I think, dispose of the contention that a smaller vessel ought to have been built and would have been sufficient for the service.

The Carson is to cost approximately $11,500,000, and not the $20 million that was reported recently in a Montreal newspaper. I have been unable to find in my department any record that suggests that at any time my officials expected that the ferry could be built for $4-5 million, nor have I found any authoritative statement whatever to this effect. Our first departmental estimate, made after an examination of the specifications with the shipbuilders, was $7-5 million, to which the builders' fee had to be added. This cost has increased to the present figure because the costs of materials and labour, which were subject to escalation, have substantially increased and because of the additions and improvements that were authorized during the construction of the ship.

After these remarks, Mr. Chairman, which I hope will clear up the misconceptions concerning both the vessel and the harbour, I want to say that Canada has formally undertaken to provide this service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. The government is going to carry out this commitment faithfully. Regular service between these two points will be provided as soon as it is feasible to do so.

In the meantime the William Carson will, within the next few weeks, be placed in service by the C.N.R. on a limited basis between North Sydney and Argentia. Because the ship is designed to fit into specialized unloading and loading facilities that are available only at North Sydney and Port aux Basques, this temporary service to Argentia will be for freight movement only and will not provide for passengers or the carrying of automobiles. This temporary service to Argentia will provide valuable experience as to the operation of this highly specialized ship and should bring about an improvement in the carriage of freight to and from Newfoundland.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that with this summary of explanations the estimates of my department will commend themselves to immediate adoption by this committee.

To come to the first subject on which I propose to concentrate my remarks today, the Department of Transport ships sailing into the northern waters of Canada. Canada's Arctic areas are becoming steadily more important. As most of the centres have to be reached by ship, the Canadian government ships sailing into the Arctic are also becoming of increasing importance. I must admit that I was startled and disappointed to read last September a report by a responsible Canadian journalist who had spent some weeks on the Department of Transport vessel the C. D. Howe. I refer to Mr. Stanley Burke. Mr. Burke is a member of the press gallery.

He served as a lieutenant with the Canadian navy during the war; he commanded an anti-submarine patrol vessel and later was navigating officer of a torpedo boat in the English channel and gunnery officer on a Canadian destroyer. He comes of a sea-going family. Mr. Burke went north last summer with the C. D. Howe and his dispatch was printed in the Vancouver Sun of September 10, 1954. This article is headed ""Canada's Arctic ship dirty and inefficient. Political appointees do slovenly sailing job."" I am going to read the first three paragraphs because I think the serious allegations set out should be dealt with by the minister. They read:

Aboard CGS C. D. Howe, at sea.-At a time when 5,000 Canadian seamen have been pulled off the high seas, when hundreds are on the beach in every port looking tor ships, the Canadian government mans its ships with inexperienced political appointees.

I'm writing this aboard the Department of Transport's Arctic patrol ship C. D. Howe. For the past three weeks I've been aboard her on the eastern Arctic patrol and I've had a chance to see her ""political"" crew in action. I hate to say this because she's a friendly ship with a few good seamen aboard, but she's dirty, inefficient and no credit to the blue ensign of the Canadian government.

That's my opinion, for what it's worth, based on three years in the navy, a deep-sea trip as a crew member on a merchantman and a lot of time knocking around the B.C. coast. It's also the opinion of passengers aboard the Howe, for whom the ship's operation is something of a joke, and for several hundred people in 19 Arctic communities who depend on her for supplies, medical care, and contact with the ""outside"".
I am not going to read Mr. Burke's dispatch in full but there are certain parts of his statement which I think are particularly significant. He says:
I can't speak for other ships in the transport department fleet, but I'd say the Howe is wide open for a marine disaster.
Here's why:

Every year she heads north with a brand new crew of political appointees, the recognized source of government crews. Almost all obtain their jobs through political influence. Few have previous sea experience.

He goes on to point out about men sitting smoking within six feet of several thousand gallons of high-test aviation gasoline and diesel fuel, sitting on gasoline drums enjoying a smoke and so on. No doubt the minister has had this report carefully studied by his department but if he has not he certainly should do so. Mr. Burke goes on:

As might be expected aboard a political ship, discipline is casual. Crew members, who argue jovially about whose member of parliament dispenses patronage most liberally, do the minimum of work required of them.
And again:
Although some officers are experienced, they are mainly the products of the in-bred government system. Although there are deep-sea officers
Supply-Transport
on the beach who have offered to serve even as deckhands, there are only two deep-sea officers aboard the Howe. Both are Englishmen in the engine room.
Not a single deck officer has a blue water ticket. Not a single officer operating in these dangerous, fog-shrouded waters could qualify as a navigator on a deep-sea ship.
X was told that one mate has no ticket at all, not even the coasting papers carried by the other
officers.

Mr. Burke pointed out that there were representatives of other departments on the ship, for example of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources, for whom he had the highest praise; members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, for whom he also had great praise; and officials of the Hudson's Bay Company. However, apparently the Department of Transport crew were one extremely bad feature of this whole operation. He continues:

Although every man is issued with a uniform, they are almost never worn. For working rig, seamen occasionally wear dirty blue coveralls but usually they turn out in multi-coloured outfits which would look more in place in a barn than a ship.

Other agencies operating in the north are highly conscious of appearances. Even on the roof of the world, R.C.M.P. constables turn out cleanshaven in uniforms. Red-jacket dress uniforms are hanging in the closets for special occasions. H.B.C. posts are immaculate. Military forces demand usual smartness. Missions are neat. Victualling of the ship is done by the chief steward under private contract. He is not required to submit a statement showing his profits or expenses. He does not have to bid competitively for the contract. The ship's canteen is also run by the steward for his own profit. In most ships this is run by the crew.

Customers estimated they were paying close to 100 per cent profit on cigarettes which came aboard duty-free. A neat profit also appears to accrue to the steward on mugups for several hundred Eskimo visitors. He's allowed 40 cents per ""lunch"". Lunch consists of a mug of tea and a couple of ship's biscuits.

I believe that that last-mentioned condition has been remedied this year and that now the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources is supplying proper box lunches. Apparently Mr. Burke could get no statement from the Department of Transport because he is reported as saying in the Vancouver Sun of June 21, 1955:

Last year I went north with the Howe and X reported that she was dirty, inefficient, dangerous and manned by political appointees. Ever since I've been unsuccessfully attempting to get a statement from the transport department.
I suggest to the minister that he should give the committee a full explanation and if those conditions existed he should let us know what

steps have been taken or will be taken to remedy them. I pointed out a few moments ago the importance of opening up Canada's north. I think that cannot be exaggerated. It may be that we would be better served if we had this work done by a coastguard, if we established a proper Canadian coastguard and let one of their responsibilities be to look after this shipping in northern Canada.

My final subject today is the Canadian merchant navy, or the lack of such a navy. As the minister knows, this question has been raised by the opposition every year since the war. When the war ended, Canada was the fourth shipping nation of the world and was also fourth in shipbuilding. At that time we urged the government to adopt a policy which would keep Canada in the front rank and, more particularly, would enable her slow wartime ships to be replaced by fast, modern cargo vessels. It was not very long after the fighting stopped that all the other maritime nations of the world adopted a policy of that kind. But Canada alone has lagged behind, in spite of all the warnings that have been given both inside this house and beyond.

In 1947 legislation was passed which set up a governmental body known as the Canadian maritime commission. Its main job was to consider and recommend to the government whatever policies it considered necessary for the operation and maintenance of a merchant marine and for shipbuilding and ship repairing industries. By the first of the next year- that was 1948-the number of deep-sea dry cargo vessels on Canadian registry had dropped to about 145 with a tonnage of approximately one million gross tons. That was quite a drop. But at that time there were still over 5,000 Canadian seamen employed in the deep-sea fleet and Canada was still in a position to export many of her own products in her own ships and to bring back the necessary imports.

By the middle of 1949, the following year, the maritime commission had submitted to the Department of Transport a detailed report which recommended that the aim should be to keep a nucleus of a deep-sea fleet of 50 ships, containing a proportion of fast, modern, dry cargo vessels. It also recommended that the shipbuilding and ship repairing industries should be maintained. That has been done largely until the present time because of big naval orders. But the recommendation for a new, modern, merchant fleet has been ignored by the present government.

From a total of 145 dry cargo vessels on Canadian registry in 1948, just seven years ago, we are now down to 18, according to the report of the Canadian maritime commission which was tabled in the house a few days
ago. The tonnage has dropped from one million gross tons to below 90,000 tons. The number of seamen has decreased from over

column2: to less than 500. That means, of course, that nine-tenths of our merchant seamen are now on the beach and will never again be available to man Canadian vessels.

column1: Out of these 18 ships shown in the report of the Canadian maritime commission, which covered the year to the 31st of March, 1955, it shows five of 10,000 tons. But I believe three of them are in effect in the coastal trade only and one of them operates out of Italy without a Canadian crew and has not been back to this country for some years. Of the 13 smaller vessels, eight belong to Canadian National Steamships, which leaves only five operated by Canadian shipping firms. There are no Canadian ocean-going vessels out of Vancouver, and the Canadian National ships are the only ones operating out of Montreal. I quote from page 2 of the report of the maritime commission a statement which shows just how serious the situation is. It says:

It will be seen that the most significant change over the twelve month period has been the diminution of Canadian-flag ocean-going shipping, pursuing a trend which began in 1949. Other than a few ships engaged in home trade voyages and sporadic transatlantic voyages, there are now no Canadian-flag ships providing overseas transportation for passengers or cargo from Canadian ports.

The minister will say that there are 90-odd of the wartime ships transferred to the United Kingdom registry, which means that they are manned by United Kingdom seamen and are subject to United Kingdom control. The only benefit that Canada gets from them is what income tax she collects from the Canadian owners of those ships as a result of their operations. All of these ships are old. I do not think there is one modern ship in the lot. The commission also dealt with that question. On page 5 they say:

At the level of freights which has prevailed since August, 1954, the operation of the Canadian ships under United Kingdom registry should, in general, give their owners cause for satisfaction. With approaching obsolescence, however, war-built ships are gravitating towards the flags which offer low taxation benefits; progressive owners in some maritime countries are deliberately eliminating the ""Libertys"" and similar type vessels from their fleets.

Page 8 of the report shows that, since November 1953 to the end of March 1955, 24 additional Canadian owned ships have been transferred from Canadian registry to United Kingdom registry. Canada has dropped from fourth place at the end of the war to twenty-first place among the shipping nations of the world, and her deep-sea tonnage is exceeded even by that of Switzerland. Hon.

members may wonder how that can be, because Switzerland is an inland nation; but the Swiss merchant fleet is nearly three times as large as the Canadian.

Then I turn to the proportion of Canadian trade, export and import, that is carried in Canadian vessels. Those figures appear also in the Canadian maritime commission report. In 1947 Canadian vessels carried over 20 per cent of our trade. In 1953, which is the last figure given in the report of the commission, they carried a little over 4 per cent of the trade. I understand that the figures for 1954 will be down to about 3 per cent. In 1953 German vessels carried 6 [DOT] 1 per cent of Canada's trade, nearly twice as much as was carried in Canadian vessels. Japanese vessels carried 3-,8 per cent, practically as much as was carried in Canadian vessels. Norwegian flag ships carried 13-5 per cent, and Panamanian ships 7-6 per cent.

Those figures, Mr. Chairman, indicate only too clearly the failure of the Canadian government to maintain a Canadian merchant marine. The policy that is still in force is that if a Canadian shipping company sells one of its Canadian-registered ships or even one of these ships which are transferred to British registry, then the money must go into an escrow fund. The way in which the policy has worked out has been this. I think there has not been one new dry cargo deep-sea vessel built as a result.

If the government is not going to adopt any sort of policy directed to rebuilding at least a nucleus of a Canadian merchant marine, I suggest that the time has come to wind up the escrow fund and to free the owners so that they may do what they can best do with regard to these vessels. But surely there can be adopted now, without any further delay, a policy which will make it possible for this proud nation to have at least a nucleus of a merchant navy, and one composed of modem ships.

Furthermore, the navy needs, as auxiliaries, merchant vessels. Yet there will be none available should there be an emergency.

Then the problem is hitting our ports. All this year we have had complaints in Vancouver about difficulty in getting ships-ships were scarce-and we have had trouble in getting shipping for our pulp, lumber and other commodities. Here we are in the position that all these goods must be carried in foreign vessels because there are none operating under the Canadian flag. If we had Canadian ships, this nation would have some control over the goods which are carried, and it would be possible to get our own products carried abroad even though foreign shipping services might be disrupted. The same is true of our imports. To maintain our economy we need to import large quantities of certain goods. At the present time we must rely almost entirely on foreign vessels to carry these imports.
That, Mr. Chairman, sums up the situation. I believe, as does the Conservative party, that the policy of this nation of Canada should be to foster the development and to encourage

We believe that to allow the merchant navy to die-and that appears to be the policy of the present government-is to leave a big gap in the development of the nation, and one which in the event of another war might be disastrous. In any event, it is a gap which is bound to handicap Canadians with respect to carrying on their trade by sea and, I repeat, it is a gap which has arisen solely through the lack of leadership on this question by the present government.

1818667,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.5,1955-07-20,93651988-2631-417c-96e4-174904755eb1,ca.m.7635,Mr. Cardin:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Members of the committee undoubtedly know that for the past three years the Department of Transport has been keeping the St. Lawrence river channel open during the winter months up to Montreal. I understand that the purpose of keeping the channel open is to avoid the costly flooding that takes place every spring at Lon-gueuil on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river opposite Montreal. I also understand that the experience of keeping the river channel open diming the winter months is interesting in that we shall be able to find out whether or not this channel can be kept open for navigation.

Right at the outset of my remarks I should like to make it perfectly clear that I do not oppose the project of keeping the channel open during the winter months. But, as I have done on previous occasions, I should like to point out to the minister that keeping the channel open in winter has caused the farmers in my constituency and in other areas along the St. Lawrence river a substantial amount of financial loss. For instance, in my constituency, many farmers who live on the mainland have considerable farm land on islands that lie opposite Ste. Anne de Sorel in the St. Lawrence river. For the past 200 years these farmers have been cultivating hay and cutting wood on these islands during the summer months. They place the hay in bales, wait until the river freezes over and then transport the crop by sleigh back to the mainland. Hon. members will realize, of course, that once the ice is broken this procedure is no longer possible. The result is that the farmers have had to press the hay and get equipment or have somebody transport the hay to the mainland by means of barges towed by motor launches. The result is that it costs as much for transportation of the hay as it does for the crop itself. As a consequence of all this, the land that the farmers have possessed for hundreds of years on the islands has now become practically worthless.
Sup p ly-Transport

I know the legal officers of the Department of Transport have stated that the federal government is perfectly within its rights, on the basis of the British North America Act and other statutes, in cutting through the ice and keeping the channel open during the winter. I do not quarrel with that, but I should like to point out that there are very many occasions when there is a wide margin between the letter of the law and justice. I am sincerely of the opinion that it would be contrary to the basic principles of equity for the Department of Transport to disregard the pleas made by the farmers and the petitions that have been forwarded by the municipalities and farm organizations of my area.

I must say that I have discussed this point with the officials of the department and we have tried to find some way of arriving at a solution. I must also say that I have had a very sympathetic hearing particularly by the minister's parliamentary assistant, but unfortunately we have not yet been able to arrive at any positive conclusion. I regard this matter as serious and urgent, and I would ask the Minister of Transport to consider it very seriously. If it is necessary I would suggest that some members of his department might visit the areas in question to see if there is some possible way of arriving at a solution that would be acceptable to everyone.

1818668,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.6,1955-07-20,64ac8c88-87af-41f6-8ffe-90fa135ebb4e,ca.m.7958,Mr. Barnett:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Mr. Chairman, last year when the estimates of the Minister of Transport were before the house I raised certain matters with respect to transportation problems having particular reference to the coastal areas of British Columbia, a part of which are found within my constituency. Therefore I must say I am pleased to note that on the recommendation of the present minister a royal commission has been established which is charged with the responsibility of looking into some of the problems affecting the coastal trade of Canada.

I notice from the order in council of the 1st of March that the three commissioners named come from either central Canada or the maritime provinces, and while I do not suggest that these gentlemen are not perfectly capable of performing the functions with which they have been entrusted by the government, nevertheless I feel I should take a little time to suggest to the minister on the first item of his estimates that the commission should focus a good deal of attention on the west coast as well as the Atlantic and central regions of Canada.
It seems to be becoming increasingly fashionable in placing a subject before the house to give a little of the historical background. In recent debates we have been 50433-109

taken as far back as the time of Magna Carta. Therefore I thought it might be appropriate if I were to attempt at the beginning of my remarks to deal with the historical perspective of transport as far as the west coast of Canada is concerned. For that reason I should like to read a brief excerpt from an article that appeared in the Comox Argus of May 4 of this year dealing with the text of a paper delivered before the Comox historical society by Mr. Stan Douglas, in which he says:

It is not generally known that the building of the Esquimau and Nanaimo Railway was linked with the terms of the confederation of Canada. Sir John A. Macdonald, the father of confederation, in his anxiety to bring about the union of all the provinces, acceded to the wishes of the people of British Columbia for a railway connection with the rest of the dominion, but in doing so was evidently not aware of the tremendous engineering difficulties which had to be overcome or he surely would not have agreed to the provision that the western terminus of the railway would be at Esquimalt, then a British naval base. The route was to be across central British Columbia, reaching Vancouver island via a bridge from Bute inlet to Seymour narrows about midway up the island. An order in council was passed to this effect at Ottawa on June 7. 1873. Premier Amor de Cosmos of British Columbia figured prominently in the negotiations of this order.

I draw this particular passage from the paper to the attention of the minister at this time for two reasons. One is that occasionally we hear in the house reference to the terms of confederation or terms of union as far as the provision of transportation facilities is concerned, and I want to impress upon the minister that some of the same considerations quite legitimately, according to the information given here about this order in council, enter into the consideration of transportation problems on the Pacific coast. The second and more immediate reason is the fact that the Minister of Public Works is now taking in hand a project to remove what was to have been the main base of a bridge from the mainland across Seymour narrows to Vancouver island, namely Ripple Rock.

I suppose I could quite legitimately argue that the federal government is by its action at the present time destroying one of the considerations of the original terms of confederation with British Columbia. Suggestions have been made to me that one way in which the federal government could fulfil its original obligations, in view of the changes that have taken place in transportation would be by the construction of a highway tunnel under the strait of Georgia to Vancouver island. However, I feel I may have to get the advice of some consulting engineers before I put forward that proposal to the minister too seriously.
Supply-Transport

Having set the historical background, and having followed the line that seems to be taken more and more by spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative party, perhaps I might come a little closer to the present day as far as our problems are concerned. Since I have been a member I have had a number of rather pressing human problems brought to my attention which have arisen, as I tried to suggest last year when I spoke on a similar occasion, out of some of the technological changes that are taking place in the field of transportation today. As a result I have tried to find out just what the present situation is as far as government arrangements are concerned. I have had some communication with the Canadian maritime commission. I notice that in the Canadian Maritime Commission Act, section 6, it is stated:

The commission shall consider and recommend to th s minister from time to time such policies and measures as it considers necessary for the operation, maintenance, manning and development of a merchant marine and a shipbuilding and shiprepairing industry commensurate with Canadian maritime needs.

Perhaps that particular section has greater reference to some of the remarks which were made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. On the face of it, one might wonder why we have to have a royal commission, when the maritime commission can do these things. However, I realize that the maritime commission has a great many administrative duties which, I imagine, occupy most of its time and energy.
Section 7 says:
The commission may examine into, ascertain and keep records of,

column2: the shipping services between Canadian ports and from ports in Canada to ports outside Canada that are required for the proper maintenance and furtherance of the domestic and external trade of Canada;
the type, size, speed and other requirements of the vessels that are and in the opinion of the commission should be employed in such services;

column1: In my ignorance as a new member I had assumed that the Canadian maritime commission would be the logical body to which to go with problems connected with shipping. However, I was not long in finding out that in fact the Canadian maritime commission has really no such jurisdiction as that set forth in the section I have quoted. It appears to be a mere fact-finding body. While it might express an opinion on what kind of facilities are needed, it has no powers whatever to see that such facilities are provided.

Then on the other hand I find that under the Transport Act the board of transport commissioners has something to do with transport by water. I know this part would be of much greater interest to some of the
people who are confronted with these problems. Unt^er part II, section 10, we find this:
The board may, subject to the provisions of this part, license ships to transport passengers or goods or both passengers and goods from a port or place in Canada to another port or place in Canada.
Subsection 4 reads:

The board may in the licence state the ports between which the ship or ships named therein may carry goods or passengers and the schedule of services that shall be maintained, but the licensee may be authorized to substitute another ship of approximately the same tonnage for a ship named in the licence.

(5) The board shall issue a licence in respect of a ship built, building or about to be built, upon being satisfied that the proposed service is and will be required by the present and future public convenience and necessity, and unless the board is so satisfied no licence shall be issued.
Then in part III of the Transport Act, section 13 reads:
Every licensee shall be governed by the provisions of this part in respect of tolls to be charged.

(2) Any tolls may be for the whole or for any particular portion of the route of the licensee. 14. (1) Every licensee shall file a standard tariff or tariffs of tolls with the board for approval and may file such other tariff or tariffs as are authorized by this part.

All this sounds very interesting until one reads subsection 4 of section 12 of the act, which says that the provisions of this part, that is part II, do not apply in the case of ships engaged in the transport of goods or passengers between ports or places in British Columbia. Subsection (b) gives the details so far as the Atlantic coast is concerned, but I shall not go into that. Under section 12, subsection 4, all the provisions which give the board of transport commissioners power to regulate and control coastal traffic as a matter of public convenience and necessity are completely wiped out. I have been compelled to point that out to a number of people who have had correspondence with me from time to time.

I have discovered that the complete freedom of operation which this particular segment of our transportation system has goes so far that apparently there is no jurisdiction whatever having control over the kind of food they may be served on ships or the conditions of cleanliness that must exist. At least I made inquiries of the Canadian maritime commission, and they informed me they had no jurisdiction in that matter. They said they would take it up with the Department of National Health and Welfare and if they discovered there was any jurisdiction there they would so inform me.

I have not heard anything more on that matter, so I take it there is no jurisdiction. I understand there is some regulation concerning the quality of the water to be carried, but nothing that has to do with the serving
Supply-Transport

of food. The only thing 1 have been able to find myself is a regulation concerning the certification of ships' cooks on vessels in a foreign voyage or in home trade extending south of the 36th parallel, which certainly does not cover the west coast area of British Columbia.

I have some correspondence here which sets forth the position in which people who are entirely dependent upon the coastal shipping trade for their supplies find themselves. It would appear to me it is a unique situation in Canada. I have sat in on some meetings of the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, and discovered that there are all sorts of regulations which cover railway transport. I know there are a good many regulations which cover air transport. But the people who are dependent upon coastal shipping for their very life are completely without protection so far as existing legislation is concerned.
This is a letter from the Mansons Landing community club which is one of the coastal islands in my constituency. It is addressed to me, and reads as follows:
Dear Sir:

We are very concerned about the soaring prices of our up coast freight rates. These extremely high rates are eliminating all sources of income to the residents of the coast and are crippling the summer resorts, stores, machine shops, poultry-men, farmers etc. People here can't afford to pay the extra cost the freight has added to home industry.

It has always been said water is the cheapest freight transportation known yet the rail freight over the mountains on grain costs us $5.00 per ton and to bring a ton 100 miles by water up coast costs us $20.05 as you can see by the enclosed letter written to Mrs. Rexford. Also enclosed are three freight bills on the same refrigeration unit. One shipped to Mansons Landing from Vancouver costing $14.34, the same shipped from Vancouver to Manson's Landing costing $11.34. A friend from Westview-
I might explain to the minister that West-view is on the adjacent mainland.

.-was in our district and offered to take one unit and ship from there as there is competition with other freight companies. This unit cost $1.03. All these units were the same and shipped in the same crate.

At one time you could get feed up and ship eggs out and make a good living here on the coast. Egg crates were brought back free to weekly shippers. One hundred boxes of apples were shipped at a time for a nice profit. The last apples shipped from here two years ago brought a profit of eight cents per box. With the present freight rates all you would get is a freight bill.

This is the reason you find so many abandoned orchards and empty chicken houses. The majority of people had to turn to logging and fishing for a living but now the logging is nearly finished and the fishermen have to go farther away to fish.

If these conditions are allowed to continue all the settlements along the coast will become ghost towns and so it is under these circumstances that we send a plea to you to aid us in the present investigation into freight rates.
The letter addressed to Mrs. Rexford, which was referred to in this communication, was from the United Milling and Grain Company Limited of Vancouver, British Columbia. It reads as follows:
Dear Mrs. Rexford:

We received your letter this morning regarding the debit note that had been sent to you covering an undercharge on freight. On checking back we found that the Tidewater Shipping Company had charged us $20.05 on your shipment on invoice No. 81831.

I phoned them to see if they had made an error, and they informed me that the freight had increased to Mansons Landing by 331 per cent on January 17, which makes the rate $20.05 per ton instead of $15.05 formerly.
We hope this explains the situation to your satisfaction.
The invoices in respect to the shipment of the freight unit which was referred to accompany the letter.

I want to make clear, Mr. Chairman, that the fact that the Tidewater company is referred to in the letter is in no sense a condemnation of that particular company as such. I am not suggesting that they are any better or any worse than any other firm operating under similar circumstances, or that necessarily their economic position does not require an increase in revenue. I have put that communication on record in detail because it does point out one problem that is being created by the changing transportation system on the west coast of British Columbia.

It does point out to me at least the necessity for this commission to make a thorough study of the situation on the British Columbia coast. I know they are going to have to consider the impact of the St. Lawrence seaway and so forth. Now that this commission has begun its sittings, I hope that the hearings on the west coast of British Columbia will not be merely perfunctory but that there will be a thorough canvass of the situation. I hope it will also give due consideration, and that the minister will recommend that they give consideration, to analysing why this particular segment of our transportation system should be left completely unregulated so that it can raise its rates by 33 J per cent willy-nilly whenever it feels like doing so, and why the question of public convenience and necessity is not a consideration as far as the establishment of transportation rates on the west coast are concerned.

As I understand it, at the present time if 20 firms suddenly decide they want to start freight lines or passenger lines to a particular area they are at perfect liberty to do so, and to cut one another's throats and all go out of business and leave the people without any transportation facilities whatever. That is the sort of thing that concerns me.
Supply-Transport
That is one of the things I feel should be brought to the attention of this committee at this time.

Last year when I spoke along somewhat similar lines I also tried to point out the complex way in which, in an area such as that along the British Columbia coast, the various forms of transport are interrelated. For example, the impact of passenger travel by air on the coast has had a tremendous effect upon the services that are being provided by coastal steamers. I also know that with the bits and pieces of a highway system developing on the coast-and some of these islands have roads-the trend today is toward the provision of automobile ferries, whereas in years gone by there was a sufficient volume of passenger and freight traffic to provide frequent and fairly adequate steamer service up and down the coast.

That volume has been decreasing because of air transportation and because of the evolving of the barge system of shipping freight, and other factors. That does not take into consideration the human situation in which people who have been well established, in some cases for three generations, on these islands, where they have their homes and their all, are left high and dry. No one has any responsibility to see that the situation is not changed. The member for the constituency is completely powerless to make representations to any adequate government body that has any jurisdiction to do anything about it.

In this same connection I had some discussions with the colleague of the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Public Works. It was in connection with the problem of automobile ferries. As the Minister of Public Works indicated yesterday when his estimates were under consideration, there are areas in which the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works seem to overlap.

I have suggested to the Minister of Public Works that there should be some new formulation of policy in regard to the responsibility the federal government is prepared to undertake in connection with facilitating the development of this new form of transportation. I feel that the demand for the traditional steamer type of wharf which has been provided for long years is declining because the facilities of the federal government are going to decline, and that it should be possible-I have suggested at least to the point of being prepared to facilitate the establishment of harbour protection facilities-to assist in the development of the newer form of transportation which I feel in many instances will be much more economical and certainly will

solve the problems of the people on some of these islands to which I have referred. If they could have some form of short-distance communication to the larger community that exists on Vancouver island, rather than having to depend upon the long haul up and down the coast from Vancouver and back as they have in the past, it would be a fairly adequate solution to their problem.

I have drawn to the attention of the Minister of Public Works one or two specific instances where the problem has become acute. One of them exists in a place called Hornby Island. I also want to make the Minister of Transport aware of the fact that Hornby Island is a most delightful place. If ever he is able to plan a holiday on the west coast and should visit Hornby Island I am sure he would enjoy the fishing and the swimming there.
I hold in my hand a letter from the Hornby Island property owners and residents association. It is addressed to the Minister of Public Works and reads as follows:
For many years this island was served by the C.P.S.S. passenger and freight vessels, but over two years ago the service was discontinued, leaving the residents here more or less isolated.

To meet their dilemma a local fisherman with the financial assistance of the Hornby Island credit union, constructed a craft-presently plying between Hornby island and Denman island-for the transportation of passengers, freight, etc., to and from this island. Furthermore, the residents of Hornby Island, at their own expense, constructed a landing on the Hornby island side of the Lambert channel. On the Denman island side an old federal government landing is being used.
Since the installation of this service, which replaces that previously provided by the C.P.S.S., traffic has increased materially, and so far, this service has been maintained without serious mishap.
Unfortunately, both the landings above mentioned are unprotected against the elements and at times berthing and docking of the craft is dangerous.
We therefore ask for the assistance of your department in the installation of breakwaters for the protection of these landings.

I feel that this sort of thing should properly be the concern of the Minister of Transport. If I understood the Minister of Public Works correctly yesterday, he said his department provides certain facilities but they are under the administration of the marine services branch of the Department of Transport. As I said last year, the Minister of Transport is the only federal minister who has within his jurisdiction the whole range of transportation facilities in this country, and is the only minister who can initiate policies which will provide an adequate correlation and coordination of transportation. A little intelligent engineering and planning would go a long way toward solving the problems many of these people are facing.

1818669,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.7,1955-07-20,fdce9d46-5c36-4ca6-b6c7-52d1e6f9ba0b,ca.m.8192,Mr. Low:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Mr. Chairman, my only excuse for taking any time of the committee at this

stage of the discussion of the estimates of the Minister of Transport is that he is a new minister and therefore is not likely to be yet in possession of all the facts which he eventually will get. There is a problem which I think should be brought to his attention now in order that he may have a chance to give it his usual careful consideration. I feel convinced that when the minister is thoroughly aware of the situation which I shall describe briefly he will feel like taking some action which I am sure will be remedial in character, and achieve that for which the people in this particular area have been looking for a long time.

What I am talking about is the plight of northwestern Alberta and northeastern British Columbia, sometimes called the Peace river blocs of those two great provinces. As the minister doubtless knows, the Peace river country is a great developing empire. I represent the section on the Alberta side and my constituency takes in approximately one-quarter of the whole area of Alberta. That fact is not commonly known or appreciated. There are now approximately 70,000 people in that area.

In order to reach the heart of the Peace river country it is necessary to travel a distance of 350 miles from Edmonton. As I say, that brings you only into the centre of the country. The whole area, both in British Columbia and Alberta, is served by only one railway, the Northern Alberta Railways, which runs from Edmonton. It is a single track road all the way which divides at McLennan, one branch going westward and south of the mighty Peace river to Dawson Creek, British Columbia, while the other branch runs north of the great Peace river into Hines Creek, which is about 80 miles from the British Columbia border.

Just what is the situation with respect to rail service? I emphasize that there is no connection between the Northern Alberta Railways and the Pacific coast. The Pacific ports of Prince Rupert and Vancouver are the natural outlets for the vast and increasing production of the Peace river country. The breaking point in freight rates on eastward versus westward hauls would be somewhere about the western end of Lesser Slave lake, which is in the easternmost fringes of the Peace river area. Since no Pacific coast or western rail outlet has been provided, all shipping is subject to the disadvantage of the almost prohibitive cost of a back-haul of more than 350 miles to Edmonton before the products can get started toward the water terminals. That in itself is a terrific disadvantage. If you expect this country to develop as it ought to and be in position to
Supply-Transport
supply the vast production which it is capable of providing for the strength of Canada, you must take note of the need of that great country for some sort of real and efficient railroad connection.

The Northern Alberta Railways were built by the Alberta government in the period prior to 1921, but were sold by the United Farmers' government to the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National Railways and are now operated under joint ownership. The railway companies were wise when they purchased the Northern Alberta Railways from the Alberta government, because they have created a monopoly that seems to be exceedingly difficult to deal with.

The Canadian Pacific had no right whatever to be up in that area, but they were wise and astute in getting in there because it gives them a share of the traffic that comes out of the Peace river country, even though their nearest main line point is at Calgary. It was well known that this was Canadian National territory, but the Canadian Pacific got in there and now command perhaps a full share or even more than a full share of the traffic which comes out of the Peace river country and lands up at Edmonton. They demand it as the price of their joint ownership of the Northern Alberta Railways.

It seems to me that the government of Alberta of that day was shortsighted. They did not foresee what would happen or what could happen, but as a consequence of what they did the only competition to the rail monopoly is truck transportation. Today the Northern Alberta Railways are trying to destroy that truck competition by the adoption of a very low rate schedule from Vancouver to Dawson Creek. I know these low rates are of temporary advantage to the people in the area, but after the truck competition has been put out of business they will bring the freight rates back to any level they want and there is nothing that can stop them except the watchful eye of the minister and his board of transport commissioners. I hope they will keep an eye on these rates.

What of the future? For long efforts have been made to interest the government of Canada in providing western outlets for the areas I have mentioned, the Peace river bloc in British Columbia and the Peace river bloc in Alberta. You can go back 30 years and find that such great men as William Lyon Mackenzie King went up into that area and just before an election promised the people that if he and his government were elected they would put through western coast outlets for the Peace river country. Those are on record and the minister can find them. These promises go
Supply-Transport
back I think over all of 30 years, but in spite of them we have no west coast outlet, which is the natural outlet.

May I point out also that in the early thirties Sir Henry Thornton made a promise to these people right on the ground. I think he was speaking in Grande Prairie when he said that if their grain production reached 10 million bushels per year he would see that they had a western coast outlet. I point out to the minister that in a normal year the Peace river country will produce and ship from 32 to 33 million bushels of grain and many thousands of head of cattle and hogs. As a matter of fact, during the war my constituency was one of the greatest hog producing areas in all Canada. There are many other products, such as timber, that come out of that area.

The promises were made, but I realize they have not been kept. I do not think the railways intend to keep them. It will be exceedingly difficult to break their present monopoly position unless the government takes a hand. As I said, because they are a monopoly they face no danger whatever from any other railway competitor. They can set their rates to be more than competitive with truck rates and, as a consequence, they do not now fear truck traffic too much. Until roads into the vast territory have been much improved they do not need to fear too much from truck traffic.

As I say, there is only one thing that can be done. I think it must be recognized that this is Canadian National territory, that its nearest terminal points in British Columbia on the western side will be Canadian National terminals. It should be recognized also that the only way you can deal with a monopoly of that kind is to have the government say to them, ""Now, we expect you to keep your promise and provide this outlet for this growing empire; otherwise we shall have to consider expropriation"". I think the government has every justification today for expropriation of that road, and when they expropriate it they should turn it over to the Canadian National Railways for operation and development. I am satisfied that under the Canadian National Railways alone we could expect to have the necessary extension provided.

I think the government would have to be prepared to subsidize the building of the railway from Dawson Creek on the south side or Hines Creek on the north of the river to some terminal on the Pacific coast. We are not making any specific recommendation in that regard at this moment, because experts will have to go in and make careful surveys to determine for themselves what is the best route. But the government will have to consider some sort of subsidy to assist in

building this railway. When I speak of expropriation as the only means of breaking the present deadlock, which must be broken, I make the recommendation with another, that when expropriation does occur or if it occurs, adequate compensation will be given the Canadian Pacific Railway, though morally they have no business in that area at all, as far as I can see.

Just recently the premier of British Columbia made a proposal to the government of Canada that his government would be prepared to extend the Pacific Great Eastern Railway eastward from Prince George, which is its northern terminal at the present time, in to Dawson Creek. They asked the federal government to give assistance. I think the government replied that certain assistance would be forthcoming. I have forgotten for the moment the exact amount.

I would think the cost of building a railroad through that country would be closer to $200,000 a mile. I believe he will find that is true. However, be that as it may, I am not now complaining so much about the government's offer except that it is just a mere pittance. Fifty miles is neither here nor there in respect to providing an outlet for northern Alberta.

This government should take a very careful look at what is happening in that area. It should remember that it is growing very rapidly, and includes just about the last remaining open spaces which can be opened

up for farming purposes in Canada. I draw the minister's attention to the fact that on the Alberta side the provincial government is now in process of opening up another two million acres of wooded land to homesteaders and helping them to get it cleared.

Unless some relief is provided, in future the people will be up against a problem much worse than they face now in my area. Every year we have a tremendous pile-up of wheat, barley and oats in that part of the country because they cannot get enough cars in there to haul it out. The big reason is that it takes too long to get in there, load up and then make the back-haul to get it into Edmonton before the grain can even start on its way either to the head of the lakes or to Vancouver. Because of that fact we have today many towns with elevators completely plugged with grain. Many farms have 5,000,

column2: or 7,000 bushels and maybe more which they cannot haul anywhere. We are approaching the 31st of July, the cut-off date for the 1954-55 pool, and the farmers will not be able to get in and participate in that pool. That all makes it very difficult for them.

column1: I say this to the minister in the hope that he will familiarize himself with the facts of the situation there and put all the pressure he can on the railways to provide a western outlet, which I am certain the facts of the situation now justify in every possible way.

I am not blaming him for what has gone on in the past. I know he has not had his hand on things before. But if he looks at the facts I am sure he will find them in accord with what I have brought to his attention today. When he sees them, I am satisfied he will be seized with the importance of fulfilling the promises that have been made for so many years to the people in the Peace river country.

1818674,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.12,1955-07-20,77e003b6-264d-4255-b8db-a088d5630f4f,ca.m.3961,Mr. Villeneuve:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Mr. Chairman, while we are on the estimates of the Department of Transport, may I, on behalf of the people of Roberval county, whom I represent in this house, thank the government for its wise decision to grant a subsidy of $7,450,000 to the Canadian National Railways, for the immediate construction of the trunk line from Chibougamau to St. Felicien, at a total cost of $17 million.

That decision, as officially announced in the house by the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) on June 3, was most welcome throughout the Saguenay-Lake St. John district, and more particularly in Roberval county.
Together with my colleague, the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier), I
Supply-Transport

missed no occasion to call the government's attention to the importance of this project, which had been the local people's dream for nearly 50 years, but in doing so I always restated my confidence in the government's good will. And today, once again, in the light of the support just received, I am happy to see that this confidence of mine has not been misplaced.

At the initial stage, that of delegations and petitions, the sympathy shown for this project by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) helped sustain the morale of the citizens of my district.

At the second stage, that of legislation, in May 1954, everyone remembers the boldness of the then minister of transport, the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, who did not hesitate to introduce in this house a bill which, necessary though it was, could then be only partially implemented, and which brought upon the minister some rather unpleasant and undeserved charges from the opposition. During that time, we, on the government side, remained optimistic without however relaxing our efforts, knowing that a responsible government never introduces legislation for the mere sake of padding the statute books.

At the third stage, when seeking some traffic guarantees, it became obvious that the requested guarantees could not be given, particularly because of the fact that there were no smelting facilities in the area concerned.

The only possible solution was a government subsidy to the railway. A new face had just appeared in the cabinet, in the person of the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), a worthy successor to his immediate predecessor. With energy, tact and conviction he set about the task, a task which had become both difficult and delicate, of bringing the negotiations to a satisfactory conclusion, and he did this in the masterly way for which he is known.

That decision of the government, I believe, has a threefold character. First, politically speaking, it means a return to the old policy of subsidizing our railways for the development of less-favoured geographical areas and for a better distribution of the country's population and resources. Second, in the economic field, it aims to establish a sound balance throughout the country, by providing each area with the means to create assets. As both the Lake St. John and the Abitibi districts are soon to be connected with Chibougamau, I trust that, before long, from the point of view of the railways and because of their complementary economies, they will show a remarkable advance. Because of the new
Supply-Transport

developments already in prospect, this line will become an unprecedented source of revenue for the Canadian National Railways, and I am sure that the government will never regret its decision in favour of my district, because this trunk line will be self-supporting. Lastly, it is an historical gesture, for a project that has been nurtured for fifty years cannot fail to make a deeper impression on the mind of a whole population when it is finally carried out.

The Chibougamau railway will remain impressed in the minds of the people of my riding as a triumphant march on the road to progress. It is almost too good to be true, and will remain all the finer for having come true. I see in this achievement the fruition of the sweated labour of our worthy pioneers. As a matter of fact, does not the attitude of our present government confirm the trust they put in this promising part of the land a hundred years ago?

Therefore, since I am the member most interested in this project and since this section of the railroad will go through my constituency up to its extreme northwest tip, I want to go on record as thanking, on this occasion, all the government members whom I had the opportunity to thank personally and if, moreover, any kudos is due to me for the outcome of this victorious fight for the Chibougamau railway, I want my hon. colleague and friend, the member for Lake St. John (Mr. Gauthier), to get at least an equal share of the credit. I owe this hon. member that testimonial of thankfulness for the support he gave me in that memorable fight.
The citizens of our district will certainly not fail to prove to the government, in due time, that they belong to a province whose motto is ""Je me souviens"".

1818683,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.21,1955-07-20,ea30e79d-1feb-461a-bbea-b3e5a570ee30,ca.m.468,Mr. Nowlan:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Of the shoals. He said the department put the terminal at a new place and then the channel was made due south of the terminal so there could be a straight run in and out. I think that is the situation, all right, and that is probably the crux of the whole problem. A new terminal was built at a place in the harbour where no terminal had been before, and to make navigation very easy the channel was made so you could get a straight run in and out to the terminal; but at the same time you also provided for the surge to get a straight run in and out to the terminal. It was all very simple, and it worked out exactly as one should have anticipated it would. With a straight run in there through the new channel, with the shoals having been blasted on either side, with the system of loading that steamer by using elevators with only a slight clearance of a few inches, and with the normal weather conditions which must be expected there a good part of the year, it is apparently considered now-and I think this is an understatement -that it might be risky to load and unload the ship under those circumstances.

The amazing thing is that according to the minister the management of the Canadian National Railways have only recently expressed some fears with respect to this matter. I think one question which must be answered is why this was done only recently, because it has been obvious for some time.

If one reads the papers published in Newfoundland, if one reads the news stories emanating from that province, if one reads the scathing editorials in the St. John's papers, it is obvious that this is not a matter of recent occurrence. It has been referred to in the press of that province for years. Even members of parliament from that province have warned the department in newspaper interviews of this result but they got nowhere. They said that when they went to the government-I presume ""government"" means the department-the government said it was the responsibility of the C.N.R., and that when they went to the C.N.R. the C.N.R. said it was the responsibility of the government.

At any rate we now have the minister, on the first occasion of presenting his estimates to the house, highly embarrassed to say the least by having a situation on his hands which never should have been created, and which I think will take a great deal of explaining before it can be satisfactorily dealt with. It involves more than the minister said this afternoon. He said it was just recently that the officials of the C.N.R. had become worried about this situation. I have here a typewritten copy of a statement which appeared in the Halifax Herald of June 28, reporting an interview with the deputy minister of transport. According to the quotation marks in that article the deputy minister said:

We had our engineers working on the project, the C.N.R. had its experts and the public works department had its technicians. The best available people worked on it and we thought what was being done would work out all right. We didn't realize what was going to happen until the work had been completed.""

Having quoted that statement, I think that is sufficient comment on the situation, and I feel the minister should explain to the house why it was not realized that this would happen before it did. To say the least, I think it does not reflect that degree of skill, knowledge and competence of which the minister of transport boasted in the house one year ago. We also want to know now what is going to be done in the future.

The minister was very good in taking certain criticisms and indignantly denying them. He said there was never any suggestion that the ferry was going to cost $25 million. No one has ever suggested that even in the wildest, most extravagant story that may have been published. What has been said is that the ferry, plus the installations at North Sydney and Port aux Basques and the dredging work done in the two harbours, would cost in the neighbourhood of $25 million.

Of course, even after all that is satisfactorily explained-that is if it can be explained1-there are still many questions left with respect to the operation of this service. There are many people down there who have had a great deal of experience in these waters and who express the opinion that this ship is not the right type to have been built for this service. That is a very tight schedule] and with the type of weather, icing conditions, fogs and all the rest of it which prevail in those waters a very substantial part of the year, it is going to be a very expert mariner who can even approach that type of schedule. On the other hand two boats would have provided a better service, at least in the opinion of many people in Newfoundland.

Mr. Chevrier, in suggesting a bridge from Nun's island to the south shore, said he felt this was preferable to a highway along the seaway dike, as proposed by the city's St. Lawrence seaway bureau in conversations with transport minister Marler in Ottawa yesterday.

The minister can interrupt and wiggle as much as he wants, but the quotations are on the record. Montreal comes along and says we think there should be a four-lane highway along the top of this seaway dike. They come back with the minister's assurance of immediate and sympathetic consideration to the new proposal and feeling, as I indicated by my quotations, that they were going to get what they wanted. In the same edition of the newspaper which reports this, we have the president of the seaway authority saying that another plan is preferable to this one proposed by the city of Montreal. If that does not indicate a certain air of dissension, a certain lack of agreement between the Minister of Transport and the president of the seaway authority, I am very surprised.

On the other hand, of course, the minister may well get up and argue that all he was doing was patting the boys from Montreal on the back and trying to get them out of Ottawa as quickly as possible so they would stop bothering him. But I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that technique is largely restricted to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who does not even want them to come to Ottawa, and would hardly commend itself to the citizens of Montreal who are perhaps a little bit more sceptical of this new minister than the people of Port Arthur were until recently. I have no doubt their scepticism is increasing at the moment. Someone points out to me that the Port Arthur delegation is coming down, but I do not know why after the telegram they
got from the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I should think an insult like the one they received would tend to keep them away for all time.

I have pointed out one small aspect of this situation in respect of the seaway in an attempt to prove to the minister the necessity for a very complete and full statement from him on what are the plans. Shovels are digging into the ground all along the south shore below Montreal. Construction work is well under way. It is high time the government, the minister and the seaway authority stopped wobbling, stopped trying to hide behind a mass of verbiage and indefinite statements, and came out and indicated what they propose to do. Certainly those people in Montreal who know the situation, who have been not too well satisfied, would like to have more information.

The seaway as such is being put through in such a way that there will be a lien of untold millions of dollars for years to come on the municipal finances of Montreal. The reason for that is that the location of the seaway is going to affect bridge construction for all time to come. Not only will it require the reconstruction of the existing bridges, but any additional bridges that will be required will face similar problems, and some expensive structures will have to be constructed in a special manner rather than the ordinary medium level bridges which would have sufficed had the seaway channel been placed in the middle of the river.

In addition, to give the minister some of the other things we are worrying about, there is the question of the turning basin when the ships come out of the canal in order to enable them to swing around and get back into the Montreal harbour. I shall deal in some detail with these plans for Montreal harbour when we come to the national harbours board estimate, but I do hope the minister will give us a very careful survey of the St. Lawrence seaway before we leave this first item.

Before I leave the seaway, Mr. Chairman, may I say there is another aspect of this matter which worries me. Apparently the seaway plans to expropriate a thousand acres in Caughnawaga for seaway purposes.

It is far more than one can take without affecting the land remaining to a very considerable extent. Second, if you consider a strip probably three acres wide, which would be some 600 feet, certainly large enough for the purpose in hand, it would work out to-I am just working it out here in order to show the rather

phenomenal length-330 acres long, and if my memory serves me rightly an acre is 200 feet in each direction. Therefore you would have a strip through the middle of the Caughnawaga Indian reserve some 66,000 feet long, or some 13 miles.

1818755,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.93,1955-07-20,d3117809-e7d1-45d2-9762-d1a2621aa271,ca.m.3975,Mr. Michener:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a continuing problem about which I spoke at some length last year. I refer to the matter of air pollution and smoke abatement in the metropolitan area of Toronto particularly, which is the area about which I am more concerned.

This problem of smoke abatement has become an important industrial problem and concern from the point of view of the health officials in the city who are charged with that responsibility, and particularly Professor E. A. Allcut, a mechanical engineer who is chairman of the air pollution advisory board of the city of Toronto. The estimate is that air pollution costs the city in the neighbourhood of $10 million, and although the figure is not definitely ascertained it is estimated that approximately 350 tons of solids per square mile are deposited each year in the city. These deposits are heavier along the railway lines and the waterfront, which of course brings me to two aspects of this problem which concern the Department of Transport; that is, railway locomotives and steamships.

As I say, this is a continuing problem. Perhaps the railways have gone some distance in reducing pollution by their dieselization program, though I feel the long-term answer is electrification because the diesel engine substitutes another kind of noxious odour for the solids which come out of the smoke of the steam locomotive. Perhaps the ultimate answer in the metropolitan areas is electrification, but much can be done to correct this nuisance by proper firing. Professor Allcut states in a letter to me that ""the railways are giving trouble everywhere. Much of this trouble is caused by unskilled or careless personnel employed in places where fuel could be burned satisfactorily.""

In support of this may I refer briefly to the 1954 report of the air pollution advisory board for metropolitan Toronto, which states that steam locomotives and railway roundhouses still continue to give trouble and that special meetings had been held with smoke inspectors of Toronto, Hamilton and Windsor, as a result of which it was proposed to make representations to the board of railway commissioners who alone have the power to deal effectively with this matter. Existing general order No. 18 under which the railroads operate was promulgated in 1908 and is hopelessly out of date. A proposed revision has been brought down by the representatives of the three cities named, and after approval by their respective councils this will be submitted to the board of railway commissioners for consideration and appropriate action. The report continues with the statement that steamships also continue to produce much smoke.

With the advent of deep-sea navigation to Toronto I suppose the problem created by steamship smoke will increase rather than diminish. There is a difficult question of jurisdiction. The metropolitan area has attempted to deal with harbour tugs and boats, but I think the over-all control must lie with the minister's department.

I should like to ask him a question and leave the problem with him at this point. Does he recognize his jurisdiction to control the firing and smoke emission from steamships on the great lakes particularly and, if so, is some active step being taken to assist the harbour cities to deal with this very acute problem? I appreciate that the railways and steamships create only part of the problem, but I assume they come under the jurisdiction of this federal department and therefore I raise the matter at this time and ask the minister to deal with it.

1818764,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.102,1955-07-20,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. Gillis:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,I am glad to hear the minister say that.
