The answer to that particular problem, 1 think, could have been given largely by the Canadian National Railways. At the last committee meeting we had the officials of the Canadian National Railways before the committee, and both the minister and his parliamentary assistant were there. I questioned the president of the Canadian National Railways as to the availability of markets, and as to how much coal they were using and where they were getting it. I have his answers, which were given to us on March 29, 1955. A substantial amount of coal is still being used on the Canadian National Railways.

The reason I raise that matter at this time is that within the past three months a very large colliery at Glace Bay, Nova Scotia, employing 730-odd people, closed down. Efforts were made through conferences held in Ottawa and at provincial conferences attended by government and company officials to keep that colliery open. The whole emphasis of the company closing that particular operation was that they were doing so because there were no markets for that coal. It was maintained that if they could secure an order for an additional 500,000 tons of coal, that mine would remain open. It closed at the end of June.

I questioned Mr. Gordon as to the amount of coal they were still using on the Canadian National Railways, and where they were getting it. I think the minister will agree with me that a community with such a huge investment as that should not be scrapped because that particular operation required an order for 500,000 tons of coal to keep it going and maintain that means of livelihood, when our own national railway system could have solved that problem by using that amount of coal from that area in preference to coal imported from the United States.
Mr. Gordon, in the answers he gave me, showed that there is a huge market in the C.N.R. for coal. His answers to me, as shown
Supply-Transport
on page 64 of the report of the proceedings of that committee, were as follows. I asked him the amount of coal they used in 1954. He said:

There are several ways of giving these figures, as we have done in previous years. You can have orders, purchases, shipments or consumption. I am giving the consumption figures. The total consumption of coal in 1954 was 4,110,560 tons. Of that, 1,016,175 tons was Canadian coal and 3,093,585 was United States coal.

Surely an effort could have been made by the C.N.R. and officials of the company in the matter of marketing an additional 500,000 tons of coal. The market was there, but it was being filled by United States coal. Surely in the interests of retaining the life of the community, something could have been worked out. It rather amused me, with that market available in Canada, to see the press announce that the premier of Nova Scotia was flying over to England to try to find a market there for Canadian coal subsidized by the Canadian government, when the Canadian National Railways, a creature of the government, import 3J million tons and burn it on our own national system in preference to allocating 500,000 tons of that coal to Nova Scotia production.

This would have solved the problem at very little cost, in my judgment, because most of that coal is used in the central region. In 1939 we were putting over 2 million tons of Nova Scotia coal into that market in the central region, which is Ontario, on the subvention we have at the present time. That continued till the outbreak of war in 1939. In my judgment if a sensible, honest effort had been made by the officials of the C.N.R. and the local company-because in the final analysis it is their problem-I think a market could have been worked out I think it can still be worked out for that amount of coal until such time as some other means is found for providing a livelihood for the people in that community.

I realize that the average member here and the average person who does not reside in a community like that does not see it as I do. To Mr. Gordon it is a matter of dollars and cents on the right side of the ledger. In my judgment the Minister of Transport is a sympathetic person, but he lives 1,400 miles away from the community affected. If he lived in that community and saw the situation as I see it he would feel exactly the way I do about it. In the light of the coal market that is available in the C.N.R., for the sake of arranging, on a temporary basis, perhaps, a market for 500,000 tons of coal and retaining the life of the community in preference of doing the kind of thing they are trying to do -find markets in the old country when we have them here-it makes poor logic.

I know the minister is new to the department. I am not blaming him for anything. I believe he has to have some considerable time to look around and get hold of all the ramifications of the department. I excused Mr. Gordon for some considerable time because he was in the same position. He took over a huge operation with many angles to it, and it took him time to get acquainted with all the different factors. But I think he has had enough experience now to be able to make a realistic appraisal of this question of trying to retain the means of livelihood for our coal industry while it is in its present transitional stage.

Huge quantities of United States coal are being imported. 1 believe that charity begins at home. I believe it is better economics to adjust a subvention rate to permit 500,000 tons of that coal to come into the central region than to pay $2.50 a ton on coal going over to Britain. Paying $2.50 a ton to subsidize an export is a tricky proposition. It has already upset things in Britain, and it will do so in any country. It is a bad principle. Under the circumstances the minister thought it was a palliative, a way out. It would perhaps provide the means of keeping that operation going.

1818778,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.116,1955-07-20,27b84d19-ac1e-40e2-9c06-e6f7e7fb20ce,ca.m.1879,Mr. Hamilton (York West):,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,In its

creation the air transport board gave every indication of being a desirable means of or agency for controlling the growth of the industry throughout the whole country. But in recent years it would appear that it no longer can be considered an impartial agency in connection with these decisions. I think most of our trouble has resulted from a hidebound adherence to a policy of monopoly at the top.

This tendency, of course, was exemplified most clearly in the decision approximately two and a half years ago in the Canadian Pacific Air Lines-Trans-Canada Air Lines air freight case which was heard by the air transport board. This decision appears to have closed the door to any hope of competition on the national level. Its reverberations have been felt right down through the industry to the lowliest class 4 group ""C"" charter air operator.

It is well to recall that the air transport board, at a hearing which lasted three weeks, heard submissions from various parts of the industry and specifically from the two major air lines which were before it. A resume of the facts covering the situation was put together by the board and was submitted, I think quite properly, to the government because it concerned a matter of national policy. However, what actually happened was not that the cabinet made a decision on the facts as adduced in the evidence and put together by the board, but that an additional hearing was called by the cabinet and attended by the two major participants, at which additional arguments or the same arguments were asked to be presented again.

In connection with this hearing, which I think was unprecedented in this type of matter, I think it is worthy of note that it was presided over, as I understand it, by the Prime Minister, and that the government-owned air line was represented by its legal counsel, his own son in law. It was held under circumstances which I would think any judge sitting on any bench in this dominion would find impossible, or in which he would feel that he was disqualified to act. But that consideration appeared to present no obstacle to this decision. Naturally the application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines to enter the transcontinental air freight picture was denied.

What has been the result? This country has waited two years to obtain a transcontinental air freight system. There is ample proof of that fact. It was two and a half years ago that the application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines was heard. But in the Montreal Gazette of April 25, 1955, there is this announcement in large type: ""T.C.A. to start cargo service to west coast"". I would ask hon. members, is that the way business expands in this country? Under our system of commercial enterprise should we not expect that business will go out and create a situation where it can make money under the competitive circumstances which exist in all other phases of our national life? No; we waited for the same service we might have had two years ago.

I might say that there was no doubt that Canadian Pacific Air Lines was in a position to inaugurate this service at the time of the original hearing. A dispatch from Vancouver indicates that two DC-6A 53-ton air freighters, valued at $1,250,000 each, were disposed of by Canadian Pacific Air Lines after the decision was handed down by the cabinet.

The second result of this decision has been the placing of a lid on the air transport business from one end of the country to the other, from the highest level to the lowest, because it is obvious that unless there is room for expansion at the top there can be no hope for smaller operators to expand in their field as well.

Third, and I think I should be able to say this, it seems that it has even placed the employees of the national air line in a position where they feel that their job security depends upon the continuance of a monopolistic situation, whereas truthfully I am quite sure they all would be better off and would have a better opportunity for advancement if true competitive conditions existed.
But it has had one good result. I think it is well worth noting that immediately the prospect of a competitive service loomed on the horizon, air freight rates in this country

dropped; and no matter what other explanation may be given by the minister, that is a fact that cannot be contradicted. I think there was a final result which probably is far more serious than the others. I believe from that date forward the high position the air transport board held in the esteem of the industry has been on a downhill ride, and I think latterly the government has made a mockery of the ability of three of the finest men I know in the civil service.

But let us take a look at what appears to be the only evidence of policy which has been available at any stage in this business. I should like to read an excerpt from Hansard of 1944, page 1573, where I find these words of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce:

The government desires the rapid development of air transport services in order, among other reasons, to offer post-war employment to Royal Canadian Air Force personnel. Canada's northland was pioneered by small operators who were content to enlarge their operations only as warranted by the development of the area they served. The government believes that feeder line operations, and pioneer lines into our northland, can best be developed as small operations. Our returning airmen will not be satisfied, in entering this new field of employment, to serve only as salaried employees. In this new medium of transportation, there must be a place reserved for small business enterprise.

Here was the beginning; here was a solid foundation for a beginning which would have provided at this stage a national air policy of which we would have been proud. As these operations expanded the question arose as to how far expansion could be permitted, and although there had been the indication of a holding down from the top we find that Hon. Lionel Chevrier, then minister of transport, stated on November 10, 1952, at the annual meeting of the air industries and transport association:

It was necessary that in the immediate post-war period competition should be virtually eliminated to allow various operators a reasonable chance to build up business without direct financial assistance from the government. Therefore, the government laid down a policy which was designed to allow each operator to establish himself unhampered by the chaotic competitive arrangements which had flourished during the thirties. As the industry developed however, this has gradually evolved to meet changing circumstances. . . . With the substantial growth of traffic within Canada it is no longer necessary to insist on monopoly conditions with regard to regional scheduled services and government policy will not forbid the gradual development on a regional basis of a reasonable amount of competition between scheduled air services. Any such development must be based upon findings of public convenience and necessity as required by the Aeronautics Act and any changes made by the air transport board in this direction will be very gradual and related to maintenance of conditions which will establish a sound economic position for the operators while ensuring the services that the public require.
[Mr. Hamilton (York West).!

Here was an indication that there might be some hope for competition in the levels below the top. As a matter of fact, in May of 1953 in the case of Maxwell William Ward, who applied for a licence with a base at Yellowknife in competition with the operator who was licensed there, this policy was more or less carried out. But that is not the end of the story. We have moved through these two steps; yet we find that in a decision of the air transport board dated November 30, 1954, an application by Associated Airways Limited to fly north from Edmonton into the Northwest Territories paralleling the lines of Canadian Pacific Air Lines on a regionally competitive basis was turned down.

But this is not the whole story. This case was heard in Edmonton, and the hearing took two days. I say to the minister that on or about October 19, 1954, the air transport board in its wisdom recorded a decision in favour of this application. Subsequently, and before this decision was published, it was changed. This decision, I submit to the minister, is not the decision of the air transport board. This is a decision which has been made after other considerations have been introduced into this dispute.

In connection with the general picture we might see if we can tie in the policy as indicated by the Prime Minister with the actual facts and the indications for the future. He, too, made a speech before the air industries and transport association in November, 1953, during the period the Canadian Pacific Air Lines application was pending. This is what he said:

I will assure you that the government does not necessarily intend to guarantee every operator a permanent monopoly in his area. Let me assure you that whichever way the decision goes now (reference to the then pending C.P.A. transcontinental air cargo application) it will not in the long run be a decision in favour of perpetuation of monopoly conditions. I have stated many times, before representatives of other industries, that the government to which I belong believes that as a general rule the public can be best served under competitive conditions. And I believe that once the air transport industry is soundly established, the decisions to be made by any Canadian government should be in favour of opportunities for competition.""

And in view of the tremendous development of our resources that has been taking place, a development which shows no sign of relenting, the demands for the services of commercial aircraft should increase to such an extent that increasing competition will be both desirable and beneficial.""

Those are the words of the Prime Minister. Let me see how close we are in actual fact to approaching those conditions. Here is an indication that we can expect no change in our system of transcontinental air service on the basis of commitments made by a company which indicates that they feel dependent on this monopoly for the success of the future operations of the company. But I wonder how foolish we can get when we talk about competition. While we are worrying about competition in this country, at the same time competition does exist and this is the type of competition we are meeting here in Canada. Here is an advertisement in the Globe and Mail of May 31, 1955. This tells you how to travel:
Fly Northwest's double-deck stratocruisers. Fastest to Portland. Fastest daylight service to Seattle.
I am wondering whether it would not be better to ensure that this type of business
Supply-Transport

stayed in Canada. If we reach the position where, because of a mental outlook, we are facing competition from outside Canada anyway, the same competition might prove to be of great benefit within our own country. I do not think we can expect relief for any of the operators below the top level in this business until such time as the government seriously gets down to brass tacks and does something about the situation.

You ask, what should we do? Well, first of all I would recommend that Trans-Canada Air Lines be removed from the control of one cabinet minister and placed back where it belongs, under the Department of Transport. There is no particular reason why this national institution should become one individual's particular baby. Section 15 (7) of the Aeronautics Act provides:

The board shall upon application grant to Trans-Canada Air Lines a licence to operate a commercial air service under such terms and subject to such conditions as will enable Trans-Canada Air Lines to perform any agreement made, under section 15 or 24 of the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act, between the Minister of Transport and Trans-Canada Air Lines or between the Minister of Transport and any corporation created under section 19 of that act.

Therefore the board, upon application, must grant to Trans-Canada Air Lines a licence. It is time this air line, too, came under the general control of the department dealing with matters of that kind instead of under the personal control of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

Second, we should enunciate once and for all a program which will give light to the operators of all companies in this field in Canada, which will give them an indication that there is no place they will have to stop on the road up. That policy will necessitate a vision that on a national basis our two largest air lines will have to face real competition and within a reasonable length of time.

Third, we must make of the air transport board something more than either fish or fowl. We should see that it is confirmed as an independent agency whose decisions will not be interfered with, as I have indicated some decisions have been interfered with in the past. It will be only with the restoration of confidence that there is no interference with that body and an indication that its quasi-judicial functions can be carried out without fear or favour that it can discharge its duties and create a national air policy for this country.

1818815,ca.proc.d.1955-07-20.16.153,1955-07-20,b1671015-8c69-4c16-9555-da7a421b4912,ca.m.8738,Mr. Nesbitt:,,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,,,Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister very briefly a matter which I feel is of great concern to all residents of all parts of southern Ontario. It is the lack of great lakes coastguard facilities. I have no doubt this matter has been considered by the department from time to time. I believe it has been raised in the house on different occasions, but I wish to raise it again and to give reasons why some sort of a coastguard service should be placed in the great lakes. The risks are becoming increasingly great as the years go by.

I understand that at the present time there are no facilities operated by the Department of Transport or anybody else to provide rescue service for persons on the great lakes. I understand that in cases of dire emergency the R.C.A.F. will provide some sort of service, but it seems to take quite a long time to get hold of the R.C.A.F. or any other similar service, and time in cases such as these may well mean the difference between life and death. In some cases the Ontario provincial police provide some sort of service, but there is nothing regular. It is provided, so to speak, through the gracious offices of the R.C.A.F. and the Ontario provincial police. There is no regular organization at all.

The great need for rescue work on the great lakes is of course during the summer months of June, July, August and September. It is needed at other times, but it is during those four months that there are craft operated by inexperienced persons on the great lakes. We have had numerous examples. You can pick up the paper every day in the week and read news items that in the southern part of Ontario that borders on the great lakes people are adrift in boats and people are drowning or people are caught out in storms. Last year we had the very famous or infamous incident when nine boy scouts drowned in lake Ontario. Let me refer to an item in the Globe and Mail of July 13. The headline reads:
Pair adrift all night. Burned rubber in a pail for a signal.
